meta.blurb: Over three million years ago, someone walked across soft volcanic ash and left a line of footprints. It may be the first road. Follow the routes that came next, carrying silk, gold and ideas, to the cables on the sea floor.
meta.bible: A single narrator speaks to the reader, curious, vivid and fair. Places: Laetoli and Tanzania (footprints about three and a half million years old), Egypt, Nile, Assur (city in Iraq), Anatolia, Kanesh, Iraq, Turkey, Arabia, Persia, Sardis, Susa, Macedonia, Bactria, Han China, Ferghana, Samarkand, Kashgar, Dunhuang, Taklamakan, Pamir, Rome, Indian Ocean, Baghdad, Tigris, Chang'an, Sahara, Ghana, Mali, Mecca, Cairo, Timbuktu, Kilwa, Venice, Calicut, Acapulco, Manila, Philippines, Tibet, Yunnan, Andes, Grand Canal, Yangtze, Suez, Panama, Moscow, Istanbul, Singapore, Pacific, Atlantic, Mediterranean, Caribbean, Africa, Asia, Europe, India, China. People (all long dead): Alexander of Macedonia; Zhang Qian, sent west by the Han emperor Wu about 138 BCE, returned after thirteen years; Ferdinand von Richthofen coined the name Silk Road in 1877; Xuanzang, a Chinese monk who walked to India in 629 CE; Mansa Musa, ruler of Mali, made a pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324; Zheng He, Chinese admiral, seven voyages 1405 to 1433; Kublai Khan, Mongol ruler of China; Marco Polo, left Venice about 1271; Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498; Christopher Columbus sailed in 1492; Herodotus, Greek writer; Mani, a Persian prophet. Peoples: Sogdians, Mongols, Inca, Swahili, Persian, Greek, Roman. Facts: the Royal Road ran about two thousand five hundred kilometres; Roman roads totalled tens of thousands of kilometres; Inca roads about thirty thousand kilometres; the Black Death reached Italy in 1347; Manila galleons from 1565; Suez Canal 1869; Panama Canal 1914; Trans-Siberian Railway 1891 to 1916, more than nine thousand kilometres; first container ship voyage 1956; first Atlantic telegraph cable 1858, lasting cable 1866. Key terms: Obsidian, Frankincense, Myrrh, Incense, Caravan, Caravans, Oasis, Bactrian, Monsoon, Monsoons, Periplus, Erythraean, Yam, Paiza, Chasquis, Galleons, Cocoa, Papyrus, Parchment, Cargo, Tarmac, Tanker, Sanskrit, Arabic, Turkish, Syriac, Buddhism, Christianity, Islam, Kola, Pilgrimage, Couriers, Middlemen, Cinnamon, Cloves, Gorge, Gorges, Haggled, Bazaars, Porters, Stations, Timetable. More places: Pesse (Netherlands), Giza, Deir el-Bahari, Punt, Uluburun, Lebanon, Jordan, Petra, Lydia, Hindu Kush, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Gandhara, Syr Darya, Babylon, Sri Lanka, Brindisi, Adriatic, Ostia, Berenike, Muziris, Begram, Palmyra, Indus, Mogao, Nalanda, Kucha, Luoyang, Talas, Belitung, Indonesia, Taghaza, Great Zimbabwe, Tangier, Quanzhou, Karakorum, Genoa, Ragusa (Dubrovnik), Goa, Lisbon, Bahamas, Potosi, Bolivia, Cusco, Tawantinsuyu, Lijiang, Ouidah, Benin, Zanzibar, Haiti, Kitty Hawk, Promontory Summit, Utah, Sierra Nevada, Vladivostok, Hudson, Niya, Loulan, Camino de Santiago. More people (all long dead): Mary Leakey (Laetoli footprints found in the 1970s); Otzi, the Iceman, about 5,300 years old, found 1991; Merer, an inspector whose logbook was found in 2013; Hatshepsut, Egyptian queen, ship voyage to Punt about 1470 BCE; Darius, Persian king; Appius Claudius (Appian Way 312 BCE); Augustus; Pliny the Elder; Gan Ying (97 CE); Miwnay, a Sogdian woman whose letter of about 313 CE was found in 1907; An Shigao (148 CE); Kumarajiva (401 CE); Faxian (about 399 CE); Wang Yuanlu found the sealed cave in 1900, the Diamond Sutra is dated 868; Cai Lun (about 105 CE); al-Mansur founded Baghdad 762; al-Ma'mun; al-Khwarizmi; An Lushan (755); Ashoka (about 250 BCE); Porus; Roxana; Zhang Qian's war for the Ferghana horses ended about 101 BCE; Sundiata Keita (about 1235); Ibn Battuta (left Tangier 1325); Genghis Khan (1206); Rubruck and Carpini; Rustichello; Rabban Sauma (1287); Bartolomeu Dias (1488); Magellan (1519 to 1522) and Elcano; Olaudah Equiano; Harriet Tubman; Samuel Morse (1844); Malcolm McLean (1956); Henry Ford (Model T 1908); the Wright brothers (1903); Ferdinand de Lesseps (Suez 1869). Terms: Dhows, Junks, Griots, Quipus, Chasquis, Salt, Silk, Amber, Taino. This book has twenty chapters of ten pages, and every claim is hedged where scholars disagree. Voice and tone: lively and clear; every date and number real and hedged with 'about' where uncertain; the slave trades and the plague are stated plainly and without gore; the story is of all continents, not only Europe.

beats.scene: Old footprints pressed into hard volcanic ash on an African plain
beats.summary: A line of footprints at Laetoli, more than three million years old, is perhaps the oldest road.

beats.scene: Scientists kneel beside a long line of footprints in grey rock
beats.summary: A team led by Mary Leakey uncovered the Laetoli trail in the 1970s: two or three walkers, about twenty-seven metres of prints.

beats.scene: Rain falls on grey volcanic ash while a distant volcano smokes
beats.summary: Ash from a volcano fell, rain softened it, the walkers crossed it, and more ash covered and saved their prints.

beats.scene: Elephants walk in single file along a worn path to a waterhole
beats.summary: Animals wore the first paths on their way to water, and early people followed them.

beats.scene: A small band of walkers crosses a dry plain towards a distant range
beats.summary: Over many thousands of years, people walked out of Africa and spread across the world, carrying their ideas with them.

beats.scene: Hunters carry shiny black glass stones along a forest trail
beats.summary: Stone Age people already traded useful things, such as obsidian, over long distances.

beats.scene: Small sea shells with holes lie on a cloth in an inland camp
beats.summary: Shell beads found hundreds of kilometres from any sea show that small treasures passed from hand to hand.

beats.scene: A lone traveller with a bow and a copper axe crosses a snowy pass
beats.summary: Ötzi the Iceman, who died in the Alps about 5,300 years ago, carried tools made from materials from several valleys.

beats.scene: A hollowed log canoe floats on a quiet lake at dawn
beats.summary: One of the oldest boats found, from Pesse in the Netherlands, is about ten thousand years old: water was already a road.

beats.scene: A worn bare track winds through green grass towards a village
beats.summary: A path begins with one walker; when many follow, it hardens into a road that shapes towns and trade.

beats.scene: A boat with a square sail travels up the Nile between green banks
beats.summary: In Egypt the Nile was the main road: the current went north and the wind blew south.

beats.scene: Sailors haul huge white stone blocks on a long wooden boat down the Nile
beats.summary: About 4,500 years ago the inspector Merer and his crew carried limestone to the Great Pyramid by river, and his logbook survives.

beats.scene: Egyptian ships unload incense trees and gold at a sunlit quay
beats.summary: About 1470 BCE Queen Hatshepsut sent ships to the land of Punt, and they came home with gold, ivory and living incense trees.

beats.scene: A heavy wooden cart with solid wheels rolls along a dirt road
beats.summary: Wheeled carts appeared more than five thousand years ago and made firm, level roads necessary.

beats.scene: A donkey in a leather harness stands patiently beside piled sacks
beats.summary: Donkeys, tamed in Africa more than five thousand years ago, became the first great pack animals.

beats.scene: A line of donkeys loaded with sacks climbs a rocky mountain trail
beats.summary: About four thousand years ago merchants from Assur sent donkey caravans of tin and cloth to Anatolia and wrote letters on clay.

beats.scene: A woman weaves cloth at a loom while a scribe reads a clay letter
beats.summary: Women in Assur wove cloth for the caravans and wrote letters to their men in Anatolia.

beats.scene: A smith pours glowing metal into a stone mould beside a fire
beats.summary: Bronze needs tin, which is rare, so tin was carried across huge distances.

beats.scene: Divers examine copper ingots and glass beads on a seabed wreck
beats.summary: A ship that sank off Turkey about 3,300 years ago carried copper, tin, glass, ivory and ebony from many lands.

beats.scene: A small stone seal carved with an animal lies beside a clay tablet
beats.summary: Seals from the Indus cities turn up in Mesopotamia, so ships linked two great river cultures by about 4,000 years ago.

beats.scene: A camel kneels in sand while men tie bundles to its saddle
beats.summary: A camel's body is made for the desert: broad feet, long eyelashes and a hump that stores fat.

beats.scene: A worker cuts a tree trunk and white resin drips like tears
beats.summary: Frankincense is the hardened sap of trees in the dry hills of southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa.

beats.scene: Camels loaded with sacks of sweet resin walk across a red desert
beats.summary: Frankincense and myrrh were carried by camel from southern Arabia to temples and palaces.

beats.scene: Smoke rises from a small bowl in a dark and quiet temple
beats.summary: Incense was burned in temples and at funerals and used as perfume and medicine, so demand was steady.

beats.scene: A rose-pink city carved into a rocky canyon, camels in the street
beats.summary: The Nabataeans of Petra grew rich by guiding caravans and charging for water and protection.

beats.scene: A bearded king on a throne receives gifts from many envoys
beats.summary: By about 500 BCE the Persian Empire stretched from Egypt to India and needed fast roads to be governed.

beats.scene: Mounted messengers hand letters to fresh riders at a roadside station
beats.summary: The Persian kings kept up the Royal Road, about 2,500 kilometres long, with relay stations.

beats.scene: A ship sails along a straight canal cut through desert sand
beats.summary: About 500 BCE Darius finished a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea, a forerunner of the Suez Canal.

beats.scene: A craftsman presses a stamp onto a small lump of gold
beats.summary: About 600 BCE the kingdom of Lydia, with its capital Sardis, made some of the first coins, which made trade easier.

beats.scene: A ship with a curved prow and a purple sail leaves a harbour
beats.summary: Phoenician sailors traded around the Mediterranean and spread their simple alphabet.

beats.scene: A young king in armour rides at the head of his horsemen
beats.summary: Alexander became king of Macedonia in 336 BCE at twenty and soon led an army into Asia against the Persian Empire.

beats.scene: A lighthouse and white buildings rise above a busy new harbour
beats.summary: In 331 BCE Alexander founded Alexandria on the coast of Egypt, which became a great port and centre of learning.

beats.scene: An army winds through a snowy mountain range in Afghanistan
beats.summary: After beating the Persian king, Alexander crossed the Hindu Kush into Bactria and married Roxana.

beats.scene: Soldiers build a city wall on a plain beside a wide river
beats.summary: About 329 BCE Alexander founded Alexandria Eschate, Alexandria the Farthest, beside the Syr Darya.

beats.scene: Weary soldiers sit beside a wide river and refuse to march further
beats.summary: In 326 BCE Alexander beat King Porus in India, but at the next river his men, away for eight years, refused to go on.

beats.scene: A stone Buddha with wavy hair wears a Greek-style robe
beats.summary: In Gandhara, sculptors mixed Greek and Indian styles, and the first Buddha statues look like Greek figures in robes.

beats.scene: A silver coin shows a king's head and Greek letters
beats.summary: Greek kings held Bactria and parts of northern India for about two hundred years, minting coins with Greek words.

beats.scene: Travellers rest beneath a shady banyan tree beside a well
beats.summary: About 250 BCE the Indian emperor Ashoka had trees planted, wells dug and rest houses built along his roads.

beats.scene: A monk in saffron robes walks with a bowl towards a distant harbour
beats.summary: Ashoka followed the Buddha's teachings and sent monks to other lands, and merchants carried the faith onward.

beats.scene: Generals gather around a king lying on a couch in a great tent
beats.summary: Alexander died at Babylon in 323 BCE aged thirty-two; his empire split, but the cities and roads stayed.

beats.scene: Horsemen with bows ride along a ridge above a Chinese frontier wall
beats.summary: Around 140 BCE the rich Han Empire was raided by the Xiongnu, nomad horsemen of the northern grasslands.

beats.scene: A small party of riders leaves a Chinese city gate under a banner
beats.summary: About 138 BCE Emperor Wu sent Zhang Qian with about a hundred men to find the Yuezhi and ask them to join a war.

beats.scene: A tired officer sits in a felt tent guarded by horsemen
beats.summary: The Xiongnu captured Zhang and held him about ten years; he married and had a son but kept his envoy's staff.

beats.scene: A weary rider enters a green valley full of orchards and vines
beats.summary: Zhang escaped across the Pamir to Ferghana and then Bactria, and wrote down all he saw.

beats.scene: A market stall in Bactria shows bamboo canes and bolts of Chinese cloth
beats.summary: In Bactria Zhang saw bamboo and cloth from southwest China, proof that goods reached there through India.

beats.scene: A lean traveller and one companion approach the walls of a Chinese city
beats.summary: Zhang came home after thirteen years with a single companion, and the emperor rewarded him.

beats.scene: Tall, strong horses with fine heads stand in a green Central Asian valley
beats.summary: The Han court wanted the strong horses of Ferghana and paid with silk.

beats.scene: Chinese cavalry besiege a walled town in a desert valley
beats.summary: When Ferghana refused to give its best horses, the Han sent two armies, and about 101 BCE it agreed to supply many.

beats.scene: A watchtower of packed earth rises from the desert beside a road
beats.summary: The Han built walls, beacon towers and garrisons west as far as Dunhuang to protect the new routes.

beats.scene: A narrow gate in a desert wall with a caravan passing through
beats.summary: Beyond Dunhuang stood the Jade Gate, where caravans left China and the long road west began.

beats.scene: Silkworms eat mulberry leaves on trays in a bright farmhouse room
beats.summary: Silkworms eat mulberry leaves and spin cocoons from a single thread several hundred metres long.

beats.scene: Rolls of silk are counted out as pay at a frontier fort
beats.summary: Silk was so valuable that the Han government used it as money and as costly gifts to buy peace.

beats.scene: Roman ladies in thin silk dresses admire themselves in a courtyard
beats.summary: Wealthy Romans loved silk, and Pliny the Elder complained about the money that flowed east to pay for it.

beats.scene: A scholar draws a map of caravan routes across Asia at a desk
beats.summary: The name Silk Road was invented in 1877; in reality there were many routes.

beats.scene: A map shows two caravan routes curving north and south around a desert
beats.summary: Caravans skirted the Taklamakan by a northern or a southern branch and met again at Kashgar.

beats.scene: A caravan crosses huge sand dunes beneath a harsh sun
beats.summary: The desert and mountains were dangerous, so goods passed from merchant to merchant.

beats.scene: A walled oasis city with a crowded bazaar beside a desert
beats.summary: Oasis cities such as Samarkand grew where water was found, and Bactrian camels carried the freight.

beats.scene: A merchant in a long coat counts coins in a market of Samarkand
beats.summary: The Sogdians of Samarkand ran much of the trade between about 300 and 700 CE.

beats.scene: A woman writes a letter on paper by lamplight in a desert fort
beats.summary: Around 313 CE a Sogdian woman named Miwnay wrote from Dunhuang to her husband in Samarkand, and her letter survives.

beats.scene: A Chinese envoy stands on a shore looking out at a wide grey sea
beats.summary: In 97 CE the envoy Gan Ying reached the sea beyond Parthia and turned back; in 166 CE men claiming to serve the Roman emperor reached China by sea.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers lay stone slabs for a straight road across open fields
beats.summary: Roman roads, tens of thousands of kilometres long, were built for armies but used by everyone.

beats.scene: A straight paved road runs through green fields with tombs beside it
beats.summary: The Appian Way, begun in 312 BCE, ran south from Rome to Brindisi and is still partly walkable.

beats.scene: A rider in a hooded cloak changes horses at a roadside inn
beats.summary: Augustus set up an imperial post, the cursus publicus, with relay stations for official messengers on the main roads.

beats.scene: A big grain ship with a square sail unloads sacks at a busy port
beats.summary: Rome, with perhaps a million people, lived on grain shipped from Egypt and North Africa to Ostia.

beats.scene: A Roman merchant ship with one big sail rides blue waves
beats.summary: Sailors used the monsoon winds to cross the Indian Ocean, and a merchant wrote a guide to the ports.

beats.scene: Camels cross a stony desert from a Red Sea harbour towards the Nile
beats.summary: Goods landed at Red Sea ports such as Berenike crossed the eastern desert by camel to the Nile and on to Rome.

beats.scene: Sacks of black pepper and gold coins on a wooden dock in southern India
beats.summary: Pepper from India was prized in Rome, and Roman coins have been found in India.

beats.scene: The ship Hermapollon is loaded with sacks and tusks at an Indian port
beats.summary: A papyrus of the second century CE lists the cargo of the ship Hermapollon, loaded at Muziris in India, worth a fortune.

beats.scene: Glass vessels, lacquer boxes and ivory carvings lie in a ruined storeroom
beats.summary: At Begram in Afghanistan, two sealed rooms held Roman glass, Chinese lacquer and Indian ivory, all about 2,000 years old.

beats.scene: Tall stone columns line a street in an oasis city in the Syrian desert
beats.summary: Palmyra grew rich by guiding caravans between Persia and Rome, and a tax law of 137 CE lists the goods it taxed.

beats.scene: A foreign monk in robes meets scholars at a Chinese temple gate
beats.summary: A Parthian monk, An Shigao, reached the Chinese capital Luoyang in 148 CE and began translating Buddhist texts.

beats.scene: A scholar translates scrolls while students copy them at long tables
beats.summary: Kumarajiva, born in Kucha, reached China in 401 CE and led a team that translated many Buddhist works into elegant Chinese.

beats.scene: An old monk with a staff walks alone across a vast empty desert
beats.summary: Around 399 CE the monk Faxian set out on foot for India, and came home by sea years later.

beats.scene: Monks in robes read scrolls in a painted cave temple in the desert
beats.summary: Buddhism travelled from India to China, and the monk Xuanzang walked to India in 629 CE.

beats.scene: A monk writes in a notebook beside a ruined stone shrine
beats.summary: Xuanzang wrote a detailed account of the lands he saw, and it later inspired the famous novel Journey to the West.

beats.scene: Students in red robes study in a great brick monastery university in India
beats.summary: Nalanda in India was a Buddhist university where thousands of students from many lands studied.

beats.scene: Hundreds of painted cave temples are cut into a long desert cliff
beats.summary: At Mogao near Dunhuang, monks and merchants carved and painted hundreds of cave temples from about 366 CE.

beats.scene: A man holds up a scroll in a sealed cave full of scrolls
beats.summary: In 1900 a sealed cave at Mogao was opened, with some 40,000 manuscripts, including a printed Diamond Sutra from 868.

beats.scene: Traders, priests and scholars of several faiths talk in a market square
beats.summary: Several religions spread along the routes, and followers sometimes lived side by side.

beats.scene: Workers press a thin sheet of wet pulp onto a screen beside a river
beats.summary: Paper, made from rags and bark, was developed in China and credited to the court official Cai Lun about 105 CE.

beats.scene: Prisoners and papermakers stand beside a river mill near Samarkand
beats.summary: A story says that Chinese prisoners taught papermaking after a battle at Talas in 751; historians doubt the details, but a mill soon worked at Samarkand.

beats.scene: Scholars translate books beside a great library in a round city
beats.summary: Baghdad, founded in 762, became a centre where scholars translated and added to the world's knowledge.

beats.scene: Shoppers browse rows of paper books in a lively Baghdad bookshop
beats.summary: A paper mill working in Baghdad about 800 made books cheap, and the city filled with booksellers.

beats.scene: Scholars at desks beneath a dome argue over a star map
beats.summary: Under the caliph al-Ma'mun, Baghdad's astronomers measured the size of the Earth about 830 and got a figure close to the truth.

beats.scene: A scholar writes numbers and a small circle on a slate
beats.summary: Al-Khwarizmi wrote about calculating with Indian numbers, including zero, and the word algorithm comes from his name.

beats.scene: A wide tree-lined avenue leads to a palace in a huge walled city
beats.summary: Around 700 the Tang capital Chang'an may have held about a million people from many lands.

beats.scene: A grid of walled neighbourhoods surrounds two large markets seen from above
beats.summary: Chang'an was laid out as a neat grid of walled wards, with two great markets that opened at midday and closed at sunset.

beats.scene: Women in Persian-style coats play polo on horseback beside a pavilion
beats.summary: Tang tomb figures show Sogdian merchants and camels, and polo, music and fashions from Persia and Central Asia became popular.

beats.scene: Smoke rises from a burning city while soldiers ride across the hills
beats.summary: The An Lushan rebellion of 755 to 763 weakened the Tang, and the western road soon fell out of its control.

beats.scene: Divers lift bowls of painted pottery from a wreck off an Indonesian island
beats.summary: A ship that sank near Belitung about 830 CE carried some 60,000 Chinese ceramics, proof of how busy the sea road had become.

beats.scene: Camels carry slabs of salt across the Sahara in a long line
beats.summary: Camel caravans carried salt south across the Sahara and brought gold back; Ghana and Mali grew strong.

beats.scene: A long train of camels crosses high red dunes in the Sahara
beats.summary: Camels reached the Sahara in the first centuries CE, and with them regular caravans could cross it.

beats.scene: A house built of grey salt blocks has a roof of camel skins
beats.summary: At Taghaza, workers dug slabs of salt from the ground, and Ibn Battuta saw houses made of salt in 1352.

beats.scene: Workers pan for gold in a stream beneath tall green trees
beats.summary: West Africa's gold came from streams and pits in the south, and traders took it north through the desert.

beats.scene: A royal court in West Africa where merchants pay a tax in gold
beats.summary: The empire of Ghana, strong by about 1000 CE, grew rich by taxing the salt and gold that crossed its lands.

beats.scene: A mud-brick mosque with wooden beams rises beside a busy market
beats.summary: Muslim merchants brought Islam and Arabic writing across the Sahara, and mud-brick mosques rose in the trading towns.

beats.scene: A hunter-king with a bow stands before an army at dawn
beats.summary: About 1235 Sundiata Keita founded the empire of Mali, and storytellers called griots still tell his tale.

beats.scene: A king in gold jewellery hands gold to crowds in a Cairo street
beats.summary: In 1324 Mansa Musa of Mali travelled to Mecca and gave away so much gold that its price fell.

beats.scene: Scholars read manuscripts in the courtyard of a mud-brick mosque
beats.summary: Timbuktu's mosques and schools drew scholars, and its markets sold books as well as salt and gold.

beats.scene: A family carries wooden chests of old books along a river by boat
beats.summary: Families kept Timbuktu's manuscripts for centuries, and in 2012 and 2013 many were carried to safety.

beats.scene: A wooden dhow with a triangular sail rides the swell at sunrise
beats.summary: Dhows with triangular sails, some with planks sewn together, rode the monsoon between Arabia, India and Africa.

beats.scene: Stone houses and a coral mosque beside a bay on the East African coast
beats.summary: Swahili port towns such as Kilwa traded gold and ivory across the Indian Ocean.

beats.scene: Tall curved stone walls stand on a hill above open grassland
beats.summary: Great Zimbabwe, a huge stone city inland, grew rich on gold and cattle, and traders brought it Chinese pottery and glass beads.

beats.scene: A young man leaves Tangier on a mule beside a caravan
beats.summary: From 1325 Ibn Battuta travelled for about thirty years, probably some 120,000 kilometres, and wrote a book about it.

beats.scene: A traveller in a turban walks into a harbour full of huge ships
beats.summary: Ibn Battuta saw enormous Chinese ships in Calicut and the port of Quanzhou, with cabins and several sails.

beats.scene: A Chinese junk with ribbed sails and a small compass on deck
beats.summary: Chinese junks had watertight compartments, and the magnetic compass was used at sea by about 1100.

beats.scene: A huge fleet with red sails leaves a Chinese river harbour
beats.summary: In 1405 Zheng He, a Muslim official of the Ming court, led a fleet of more than two hundred ships and about 27,000 men.

beats.scene: A giant treasure ship dwarfs smaller boats beside it in a harbour
beats.summary: Chinese records describe treasure ships about 120 metres long; historians argue that they were smaller, but they were the biggest ships of their time.

beats.scene: A giraffe stands on the deck of a ship beside a curious crowd
beats.summary: A giraffe from Africa reached the Chinese court in 1414 and was welcomed as a lucky creature called a qilin.

beats.scene: Great ships lie idle in a quiet harbour at dusk
beats.summary: After the seventh voyage ended in 1433, China stopped the great fleets, and the sea road stayed open for others.

beats.scene: A rider in felt and fur raises a banner on a windy grass plain
beats.summary: In 1206 the Mongol leader Temujin united the tribes of the steppe and took the title Genghis Khan.

beats.scene: Horsemen in fur hats gallop across a vast grassland with banners flying
beats.summary: In the thirteenth century the Mongols built a huge land empire that made the roads safer.

beats.scene: A lone trader walks calmly along a road past a Mongol guard post
beats.summary: Under Mongol rule the roads were safer; it was said that a traveller could cross the empire with gold and come to no harm.

beats.scene: A galloping rider hands a message to a fresh rider at a station
beats.summary: The Mongols ran a relay system, the yam, and gave officials metal tablets called paizas.

beats.scene: A great silver tree pours drinks in a palace hall
beats.summary: At Karakorum, a French goldsmith built a silver tree that poured drinks, as the friar William of Rubruck reported.

beats.scene: A friar in a brown robe rides beside a Mongol guide across the steppe
beats.summary: Friars such as Carpini in 1246 and Rubruck in 1253 travelled to the Mongol court and wrote the first European accounts.

beats.scene: Officials stamp red seals on sheets of paper money in a market
beats.summary: Kublai Khan, who ruled China from 1271, used paper money, and Marco Polo marvelled that a sheet of paper could buy goods.

beats.scene: A young merchant from Venice rides towards the camp of a great khan
beats.summary: About 1271 Marco Polo left Venice for China; historians doubt some of what he wrote.

beats.scene: A prisoner dictates his story to a writer in a dim Genoese cell
beats.summary: About 1298 Marco Polo dictated his story to a writer named Rustichello, and the book was copied by hand into many languages.

beats.scene: A monk in dark robes meets a pope and kings in a candlelit hall
beats.summary: Rabban Sauma, a Christian monk born near Beijing, travelled to Europe in 1287 and 1288 and met kings and the pope.

beats.scene: A merchant ship enters a harbour while townspeople watch from the quay
beats.summary: The Black Death travelled along trade routes and reached Italy in 1347.

beats.scene: A ship rides at anchor offshore flying a yellow flag while townspeople watch
beats.summary: In 1377 Ragusa made arriving ships wait thirty days, and Venice later made it forty, which gave us the word quarantine.

beats.scene: Labourers in a field talk with a landowner about their pay
beats.summary: With so many dead, workers were scarce, and in much of Europe the survivors found that wages rose.

beats.scene: Sacks of cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg and pepper stand in a spice market
beats.summary: Spices came from far away, and cloves and nutmeg grew only on a few small islands in what is now Indonesia.

beats.scene: Workers build galleys side by side in a vast Venetian shipyard
beats.summary: Venice grew rich as the gateway for spices, and its Arsenal shipyard could build ships almost like a factory.

beats.scene: A small ship with red-cross sails rounds a stormy rocky cape
beats.summary: Portuguese captains sailed farther down Africa each year, and in 1488 Bartolomeu Dias rounded its southern tip.

beats.scene: Merchants unload sacks of pepper and cloves on a bustling Venetian quay
beats.summary: European merchants wanted spices directly, and in 1498 Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa to Calicut.

beats.scene: A Portuguese captain in a plumed hat bows before an Indian ruler
beats.summary: In Calicut the ruler was unimpressed by Gama's cheap gifts, but a pilot who knew the monsoon had guided him across the ocean.

beats.scene: Portuguese cannon fire on a harbour fort while merchant ships flee
beats.summary: The Portuguese used cannon to seize ports such as Goa in 1510 and Malacca in 1511 and to force others to buy their permits.

beats.scene: A busy riverside market in Lisbon is piled with sacks of pepper
beats.summary: Lisbon became a great spice market, though Venice kept trading and the old routes did not vanish overnight.

beats.scene: A sailor studies a map at a table while a queen listens
beats.summary: Columbus believed Asia lay a short way west, and after years of asking he persuaded the rulers of Spain to pay for ships.

beats.summary: China needed Tibetan horses for its armies, so officials fixed how many bricks of tea would buy a horse.

beats.scene: A caravan of mules enters a stone-paved town beneath snowy peaks
beats.summary: Towns such as Lijiang grew rich as stops on the Tea Horse Road, and their old stone streets are still walked today.

beats.scene: A runner crosses a swaying rope bridge over a deep gorge in the Andes
beats.summary: The Inca built about thirty thousand kilometres of roads without wheels and used relay runners.

beats.scene: A stone city with four roads leaving it towards distant mountains
beats.summary: The Inca called their empire the land of four quarters, and four main roads led out from the capital, Cusco.

beats.scene: A runner blows a conch shell as the next runner leaps up
beats.summary: Runners called chasquis waited at small huts along the road and passed messages by relay, so news could travel very far in a day.

beats.scene: A record keeper reads a bundle of coloured knotted cords

beats.scene: Villagers weave grass ropes and stretch them across a deep gorge

beats.scene: A line of people walks across a desert, watched by armed men

beats.scene: A harbour with dhows and a stone town on the island of Zanzibar

beats.scene: A sailing ship leaves a stone fort on the coast of West Africa

beats.scene: Rows of people lie packed in the dark hold of a ship
beats.summary: On the Middle Passage people were packed in the holds; more than a million died before reaching land.

beats.scene: Workers cut sugar cane in a hot field watched by a rider
beats.summary: Enslaved people were forced to grow sugar, cotton, tobacco and coffee, and the profits made ports such as Liverpool and Bristol rich.

beats.scene: A group of people walk at night through a forest towards hidden hills
beats.summary: Enslaved people resisted by revolt, escape and hidden communities, and in Haiti a revolution ended slavery and founded a free republic in 1804.

beats.scene: Crowds outside a parliament building hold petitions and banners
beats.summary: Campaigners, including the former slave Olaudah Equiano, helped to persuade Britain to ban the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in its empire in 1833.

beats.scene: A lantern lights a forest path as people follow a quiet guide

beats.scene: A memorial arch stands on a quiet beach beneath a pale sky

beats.scene: A barge glides along a canal beside stone embankments and willow trees

beats.scene: A mule walks along a towpath pulling a canal boat towards a lock
beats.summary: The Erie Canal, opened in 1825, linked the Great Lakes to New York and made freight far cheaper.

beats.scene: A black steam engine pulls open wagons along an early railway
beats.summary: In 1825 the Stockton and Darlington Railway in England carried passengers by steam locomotive, and the Liverpool and Manchester line followed in 1830.

beats.scene: A paddle steamer with a tall smoking funnel crosses a grey Atlantic
beats.summary: In 1838 the steamship Great Western crossed the Atlantic in about fifteen days, much faster than most sailing ships.

beats.scene: Passengers read a station clock beside a printed timetable

beats.scene: A train crosses an iron bridge over a wide Indian river
beats.summary: India's first passenger railway opened in 1853, and the network grew quickly, built under British rule to move troops and raw materials as well as people.

beats.summary: On 10 May 1869 at Promontory Summit in Utah the two halves of the first American coast-to-coast railway met, cutting a journey of months to about a week.

beats.scene: Chinese workers lay track through a snowy mountain cutting

beats.scene: A green train crosses a frozen river between birch forests

beats.scene: A busy station hall with an arched glass roof and crowded platforms

B1B2: At a place called Laetoli in Tanzania, a line of footprints has stayed in hardened volcanic ash for more than three million years. They were made by early relatives of ours, and you could call them the first road on Earth.
In the 1970s, a team led by the scientist Mary Leakey uncovered the trail at Laetoli. It is about twenty-seven metres long and was made by two or three walkers who stayed close together.
A nearby volcano had covered the plain in fine ash, and then a light rain made it damp and soft. The walkers crossed it before it dried, and soon more ash buried their prints and kept them safe.

Long before people built anything, deer, elephants and other animals wore narrow paths through the land on their way to water. Hunters followed these tracks, because an animal's path usually leads to something useful.

Over many thousands of years, small groups of modern humans walked out of Africa and into Asia and Europe. They followed rivers and coasts, and they carried their tools, their languages and their stories with them.

Long before towns or money, people carried useful things from far away. Shiny black volcanic glass called obsidian, which makes very sharp blades, was passed from hand to hand across hundreds of kilometres.

Archaeologists have found beads made of sea shells in camps and graves hundreds of kilometres from any coast. Few people would walk that far for one bead, so the shells must have passed from one group to the next.
In 1991, hikers found the body of a man who had died in the Alps about 5,300 years ago. The man, called Ötzi, carried a copper axe and tools made of stone from places far apart.
One of the oldest boats ever found is a canoe from Pesse, in the Netherlands, made about ten thousand years ago. It was carved from a single pine trunk, and it shows that water was already a road.
A path begins when one person finds a good way across the land. When many others follow, the grass dies, the soil hardens, and the track becomes something every traveller can trust.
In ancient Egypt, the Nile river was the main road for people, grain and stone. The current carried boats north, and a steady wind from the north let sailors travel south again with their sails up.

About 4,500 years ago, an inspector named Merer led a crew of boatmen who carried white limestone down the Nile to the Great Pyramid at Giza. His logbook, written on papyrus, was found in 2013 beside the Red Sea.

About 1470 BCE the Egyptian queen Hatshepsut sent five ships down the Red Sea to a land called Punt. They came home with gold, ivory and living incense trees, and the voyage was carved on the walls of her temple.
Wheeled carts appeared more than five thousand years ago, and they changed what a road had to be. A footpath was good enough for a walker, but a cart needed a wide, firm and fairly level track.

People in northeast Africa tamed the wild ass more than five thousand years ago, and the donkey became the first great pack animal. It could carry a heavy load for days on poor food, and it was sure-footed on rocky ground.

About four thousand years ago, merchants from the city of Assur sent donkeys loaded with tin and cloth across the mountains to Anatolia. We know this because they wrote business letters on clay, and thousands of them have survived.

Some of the clay letters were written by women, because the trade was a family business. Wives in Assur wove cloth at home, sent it on the caravans and wrote to their husbands about prices and family news.

Bronze, the metal of ancient tools and swords, is made by mixing copper with a little tin. Tin was rare in the Middle East, so it had to be carried across mountains and deserts for hundreds of kilometres.

About 3,300 years ago a ship sank off the coast of Turkey, near a place now called Uluburun. Divers have recovered tonnes of copper, tin and glass, together with ivory, ebony and other precious things from many lands.

The cities of the Indus valley, in what is now Pakistan and India, made small stone seals carved with animals and signs. Some of them have been found in Mesopotamia, which shows that ships and caravans linked the two regions about 4,000 years ago.

The camel is a remarkable desert traveller, because its body seems to have been designed for dry country. Its wide feet stay on top of soft sand, its eyelashes keep out the dust, and it can go for days without a drink.
Frankincense comes from the sap of trees that grow in the dry hills of southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa. Workers cut the bark, and the milky sap slowly hardened into small drops like tears.

In southern Arabia, people collected the sticky sap of certain trees and burned it as incense. Camels carried it north across the desert to temples and palaces, and this was one of the first long-distance trades.
In temples, palaces and homes, sweet smoke was burned to honour the gods and to hide bad smells. Because the trees grew in just a few regions, the supply was small and the price was high.

The Nabataeans, an Arab people, built the rock-cut city of Petra, in what is now Jordan, on the incense routes. They knew where every well was hidden, and they earned money by guiding caravans and selling water and protection.

By about 500 BCE the Persian Empire stretched from Egypt to the edge of India, and it was the largest the world had yet seen. Its kings could rule such a huge area only if their orders travelled quickly.

The Royal Road of the Persian kings ran for about two thousand five hundred kilometres, from Sardis to Susa. Riders passed messages from one station to the next, and they changed their tired horses for fresh ones.
About 500 BCE, the Persian king Darius finished a canal that joined the Nile to the Red Sea. Ships could now sail from Egypt to Persia, and the king had the work recorded on stone monuments.

About 600 BCE the kingdom of Lydia, whose capital was Sardis, made some of the first coins from a natural mix of gold and silver. A small stamped lump of metal was far easier to carry and count than a sack of grain.

The Phoenicians, who lived on the coast of what is now Lebanon, sailed around the Mediterranean selling cloth dyed purple. Their simple alphabet of about twenty-two letters spread with their ships and became the ancestor of many later alphabets.
Alexander became king of Macedonia in 336 BCE, when he was only twenty. Two years later he led an army across the sea into Asia to challenge the great Persian Empire.
In 331 BCE Alexander founded a new city on the Egyptian coast and gave it his own name. In time, Alexandria became a great port, with a famous lighthouse and a huge library.

After defeating the Persian king, Alexander marched east and crossed the snowy Hindu Kush mountains into Bactria, in what is now Afghanistan. There, in 327 BCE, he married Roxana, the daughter of a local nobleman.
Near the Syr Darya river in Central Asia, about 329 BCE, Alexander founded a city called Alexandria Eschate, which means the farthest. Some wounded soldiers and local people were settled there.

In 326 BCE Alexander led his army into northern India and fought a great battle against the king Porus. At the next river his soldiers, who had been away from home for eight years, refused to march any farther.
In the region of Gandhara, now in Pakistan and Afghanistan, sculptors mixed Greek and Indian styles. Their statues of the Buddha have wavy hair and folded robes that look a little like Greek art.

After Alexander died, Greek kings kept control of Bactria and, later, parts of northern India for about two hundred years. They struck fine silver coins with their portraits and Greek words, and hundreds survive.
About 250 BCE the Indian emperor Ashoka ordered shade trees to be planted and wells to be dug beside his roads. He also had rest houses built, so that travellers and animals could stop in comfort.
Ashoka himself followed the teachings of the Buddha, and he sent monks as messengers to places such as Sri Lanka. Their journeys began a long tradition in which faith followed the trade routes.

Alexander died in Babylon in 323 BCE, when he was only thirty-two years old. His generals divided his empire among themselves, but the cities and roads that he had begun kept the east and west connected.

By about 140 BCE the Han Empire was rich and strong, but it was often raided by the Xiongnu, a nomad people of the northern grasslands. Their riders could shoot arrows from horseback and vanish before an army arrived.

Emperor Wu heard that a people called the Yuezhi, whom the Xiongnu had driven away, now lived far to the west. About 138 BCE he sent an officer named Zhang Qian, with about a hundred men, to ask them to join a war.
Zhang Qian had hardly left China when Xiongnu horsemen captured him. They held him for about ten years, and he married a Xiongnu woman and had a son, but he never gave up his mission.

After his escape, Zhang Qian crossed the Pamir mountains and reached Ferghana, a green valley with walled towns and fields of grapes. He then visited Bactria, where he found farmers, traders and busy markets.

In a market in Bactria, Zhang Qian saw bamboo canes and cloth that he knew came from southwest China. The merchants told him that these goods had come by way of India, so a trade route already existed.
Zhang Qian was captured again on the way back, but he escaped once more and reached the capital after thirteen years. Of the hundred men who set out, only he and one companion came home.
Zhang Qian had seen fine, powerful horses in the valley of Ferghana, and the Han court wanted them for its cavalry. China paid with silk, and so the long trade between east and west began to grow.

When the ruler of Ferghana refused to sell his best horses, the Han emperor sent an army across the desert to take them. The first attempt failed, but a second army besieged the city in about 101 BCE, and Ferghana agreed to give many horses.

To protect the new routes, the Han extended their walls and watchtowers far into the western desert, as far as Dunhuang. Soldiers lit fires on the towers to warn of raiders, and they also checked the goods of passing merchants.

West of Dunhuang stood a fortified gate called the Jade Gate, because jade from the west entered China there. Travellers who passed through it left the safety of the empire and entered the dangerous deserts beyond.
The silkworm is the caterpillar of a small moth, and it feeds on the leaves of the mulberry tree. When it is ready, it spins a cocoon from a single thread that can be several hundred metres long.
Silk was so valuable that the Han government paid soldiers and officials with rolls of it. It also sent huge gifts of silk to the Xiongnu leaders, hoping to keep the peace.

By the first century CE, rich Romans wore silk because it was light, soft and almost see-through. Some writers, such as Pliny the Elder, complained that Rome was losing huge amounts of gold to buy it.
The name Silk Road was invented in 1877 by a German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen. In fact there was never one road, but a web of many routes that changed with the seasons and the wars.
Merchants never tried to cross the middle of the Taklamakan desert. Caravans took a northern route along the Tian Shan mountains or a southern route beside the Kunlun mountains.

The Taklamakan desert and the high mountain passes were hard and dangerous to cross. Most traders travelled only one stretch and sold their goods on to the next merchant, so silk passed through many hands.
Along the routes, cities grew up wherever there was water, such as Samarkand, Kashgar and Dunhuang. Their markets sold goods from many lands, and the two-humped Bactrian camel carried much of it.

From about 300 to 700 CE, the Sogdians, who came from the area around Samarkand, ran much of the trade across Central Asia. They set up small trading communities as far east as China and spoke several languages.
Around 313 CE, a Sogdian woman named Miwnay, living in Dunhuang, wrote to her husband in Samarkand. Her letter was found in a watchtower in 1907, and it begs him to send help.

In 97 CE the envoy Gan Ying reached the sea beyond Parthia, but sailors warned him that the voyage to Rome could take two years. He turned back, but Chinese records say that men claiming to serve the Roman emperor reached the Han court by sea in 166 CE.
The Romans built tens of thousands of kilometres of roads, many of them paved with stone. They were made for marching armies, but merchants, messengers and travellers used them too.

The Appian Way, begun in 312 BCE, ran south from Rome and was later extended to the port of Brindisi on the Adriatic coast. Parts of it are still used today, and the Romans called it the queen of roads.

The first emperor, Augustus, set up an imperial post called the cursus publicus. Stations along the main roads kept fresh horses and rooms for officials, so urgent news travelled far faster than a walker could.

By the first century CE, Rome may have had a million people, and it could feed them only with imported grain. Huge ships carried it across the Mediterranean from Egypt and North Africa to the port of Ostia.
In the Indian Ocean, the winds change direction with the seasons. Sailors learned to ride them, sailing east in summer and west in winter, so that ships could cross the sea in a few weeks.
Ships from India landed their cargoes at Red Sea ports such as Berenike. Camels then carried the goods for many days across the desert to the Nile, where boats took them down to Alexandria.
Black pepper grows in southern India, and Roman cooks loved it. Roman coins have been found in many parts of southern India, which shows that a great deal of gold travelled east in payment.

A broken papyrus from the second century CE records the cargo of a ship called the Hermapollon, which sailed from Muziris in India to Egypt. It lists valuable goods such as ivory and scented oils, and the total value was enormous.

In the 1930s, archaeologists at Begram, in Afghanistan, opened two sealed rooms in an ancient palace. Inside were Roman glass, carved Indian ivory and Chinese lacquer boxes, all about 2,000 years old.
Palmyra, in the Syrian desert, was an oasis city where caravans stopped on their way to the Roman Empire. A stone tablet from 137 CE lists the taxes on goods such as oil, dyed wool and perfume.
In 148 CE a Parthian monk named An Shigao reached the Chinese capital, Luoyang. He learned Chinese and spent many years translating Buddhist texts, which were passed from hand to hand.
Kumarajiva was born in the oasis town of Kucha, and in 401 CE he was brought to China. There he led a team that translated many Buddhist books into smooth, elegant Chinese.

Around 399 CE a Chinese monk named Faxian, already in his sixties, set out on foot to find the Buddhist books of India. He crossed the desert and the mountains, and years later he sailed home across the sea.

Merchants and monks carried the teachings of the Buddha from India across Central Asia to China. In 629 CE, a Chinese monk named Xuanzang set out to walk to India, and he came home sixteen years later with hundreds of Buddhist texts.

On his return, Xuanzang wrote a detailed account of the kingdoms, customs and cities that he had seen. It is still valuable to historians, and it later inspired a famous Chinese adventure novel, Journey to the West.

In north India, the monastery of Nalanda worked like a great university, with thousands of students and teachers. Xuanzang studied there, and so did scholars from Korea, Tibet and other distant lands.
Near Dunhuang, travellers began to carve cave temples into a long cliff about 366 CE. Over the next thousand years, artists painted hundreds of caves with Buddhas, dancers and scenes from daily life.

In 1900, a Daoist priest named Wang Yuanlu discovered a sealed cave at Mogao full of manuscripts, hidden about a thousand years earlier. One of them is a printed book of 868, the Diamond Sutra, which is the oldest dated printed book in the world.

Goods were not the only things that travelled along these roads. Several religions, including Buddhism, Christianity and Islam, also spread along the routes, and in some towns their followers lived side by side.

Paper was made in China from old rags, bark and plant fibres, which were beaten into a wet pulp and spread on a screen. A court official named Cai Lun is traditionally credited with improving it about 105 CE.

For centuries China kept the craft of papermaking to itself, but it did not stay secret forever. A story says that prisoners taught it after a battle at Talas in 751, though historians doubt the details.
Baghdad was founded in 762 as a round city on the river Tigris. Its scholars translated books from Greek, Persian and Indian languages into Arabic, and they added discoveries of their own.

Paper was far cheaper than parchment, which was made from animal skin, so many more books could be copied. By about 800 a paper mill was working in Baghdad, and writers of the time describe streets of booksellers.

Under the caliph al-Ma'mun, astronomers from Baghdad measured the size of the Earth about the year 830. Scholars still debate their exact units, but their result seems to have been remarkably close to the truth.

Al-Khwarizmi, a scholar who worked in Baghdad, wrote about how to calculate with the Indian numbers, including a small circle for zero. His name, spelled in Latin, gave us the word algorithm, and the numbers spread to Europe.
Around the year 700, the Chinese capital Chang'an may have held as many as a million people. Merchants and envoys from Persia, India, Korea and Japan walked its wide streets.

Chang'an was laid out as a huge grid of straight streets, with walled neighbourhoods like chessboard squares. Two great markets, one in the east and one in the west, opened at midday and closed at sunset.
Tang fashion copied the foreigners who filled the city. People wore Persian-style coats and listened to music from Central Asia, and polo, a game from Persia, was loved at court, even by noble women.

In 755 a general named An Lushan, who had a Sogdian and Turkic background, rose against the Tang emperor. The rebellion lasted for eight years, and it left the empire too weak to hold the western road.
Around 830 CE an Arab ship sank off the island of Belitung, in Indonesia, on its way home from China. Fishermen found it in 1998, and it held about 60,000 pieces of Chinese pottery, gold and silver.
Camels also crossed the Sahara desert, carrying salt south and bringing gold back north. Great empires grew in West Africa, such as Ghana and Mali, partly by controlling this trade.
Before camels, crossing the Sahara was very hard, because horses and oxen needed too much water. In the first centuries CE camels arrived from the east, and regular caravans became possible.

At Taghaza, a mining settlement in the Sahara, workers dug great slabs of salt from the ground. The traveller Ibn Battuta visited in 1352 and saw houses and a mosque built of salt, with roofs of camel skin.

The gold of West Africa came from rivers and shallow pits in the forest lands of the south. Traders carried it north across the Sahara, and much of the gold in medieval coins is believed to have come from there.
The empire of Ghana was strong by about 1000 CE, and it lay north-west of the modern country of the same name. Its kings grew rich by taxing the salt and gold that passed through their lands.

Muslim merchants from North Africa brought their faith and the Arabic language across the Sahara. In the trading towns of West Africa they built mosques of mud brick, and kings and scholars began to learn Arabic.
About 1235 a ruler named Sundiata Keita defeated his enemies and founded the empire of Mali. Singing storytellers, called griots, have told his story for hundreds of years.
In 1324, Mansa Musa, the ruler of Mali, made a famous journey to Mecca. He gave away so much gold in Cairo that, according to reports, its value fell for years.

Timbuktu stood where the desert met the Niger river, and it grew into a famous city of mosques, schools and markets. Scholars came to study law, medicine and astronomy, and books were among the goods for sale.

Tens of thousands of old manuscripts from Timbuktu survive, because families kept them in chests for generations. In 2012, when armed fighters took the city, people secretly carried many of them to safety.
Arab, Indian and African sailors crossed the Indian Ocean in dhows, wooden ships with triangular sails. Some early dhows had planks sewn together with cord, which let them bend a little in the waves.
On the East African coast, ports such as Kilwa traded gold, ivory and timber with Arabia, India and China. Archaeologists have found Chinese pottery in the ruins of their stone houses.

Great Zimbabwe, in southern Africa, was a huge stone city that flourished from about 1100 to 1450. Its people grew rich from gold and cattle, and traders from the coast brought them Chinese pottery and glass beads.

In 1325, a young man named Ibn Battuta left Tangier, in Morocco, intending to make a pilgrimage to Mecca. He kept travelling for about thirty years, probably covering some 120,000 kilometres, and then he dictated a book about it.
In the harbours of India and China, Ibn Battuta saw enormous Chinese ships, which he said had many sails and even small private cabins. He wrote that the biggest ships carried hundreds of men.

Chinese ships called junks had strong walls inside the hull, so that a leak in one part did not sink the whole ship. By about 1100 sailors were also using the magnetic compass to find their way at sea.

In 1405 the Ming emperor chose Zheng He, a Muslim official of his court, to lead a great fleet across the Indian Ocean. Chinese records say that it had more than two hundred ships and about 27,000 men.

Chinese records describe huge treasure ships, up to about 120 metres long, with nine masts. Many historians believe that real ships were somewhat smaller, but they were still bigger than any ship in Europe.
In 1414 a giraffe from Africa reached the Chinese court as a gift for the emperor. The courtiers compared it to the qilin, a lucky animal from old stories, and artists painted it.

Zheng He's seventh voyage ended in 1433, and soon afterwards the Chinese government stopped sending out great fleets. Historians still debate why, but the sea roads of the Indian Ocean were left open for others.

The Mongols were herders who lived on the wide grasslands of the steppe, and they learned to ride before they could properly walk. In 1206 a leader named Temujin united their tribes and took the title Genghis Khan.
In the thirteenth century, the Mongols conquered lands from China to Eastern Europe. Their conquests were often brutal, but travellers found the roads across their empire safer than before.

After the conquests, the Mongol rulers punished robbers severely, and travellers could go much farther without paying a dozen different local lords. It was even said that a person could cross the empire carrying gold and be safe.

The Mongols ran a relay system called the yam, with stations where riders could change horses and rest. Officials carried a metal tablet, called a paiza, that told everyone along the road to give them food and fresh horses.

Karakorum, the Mongol capital, was a city of tents with a few grand halls. In the palace stood a silver tree that poured wine and other drinks from its branches, made by a French goldsmith named Guillaume Boucher.

Rulers in Europe sent friars to meet the Mongols, and two of them, Carpini and Rubruck, wrote the first eyewitness accounts. Their journeys took place in 1246 and 1253, and they described the food, the tents and the customs of the Mongols.

Kublai Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, became the ruler of China, and from 1271 his dynasty was called the Yuan. His government used paper money, which amazed European visitors who were used to heavy gold and silver coins.

Around 1271, a young Venetian named Marco Polo set out for China with his father and uncle. His book about the journey became famous, although some historians doubt that he saw everything he described.
After he came home, Marco Polo was captured in a war and spent time in a prison in Genoa. There, about 1298, he told his story to a fellow prisoner named Rustichello, who wrote it down.
Rabban Sauma was a Christian monk born in or near Beijing. In 1287 and 1288, he travelled to Europe on a mission for the Mongol ruler of Persia, and he met kings and the pope.
Roads carry bad things as well as good ones. In 1347, ships carried the Black Death to Italy, and within a few years it had killed millions of people.

In 1377 the port of Ragusa, now called Dubrovnik, made arriving ships wait for thirty days before anyone could land. Venice later made the wait forty days, and the Italian word for forty gave us the word quarantine.
After the plague, there were far fewer workers in Europe, and in many places the survivors could ask for better pay. Trade recovered over the following decades, and the towns slowly grew again.

Pepper and cinnamon came from India and Sri Lanka, but cloves and nutmeg grew only on a few small islands in what is now Indonesia. They crossed thousands of kilometres of sea before they reached Europe.
Venice bought spices from the Arab merchants of Egypt and sold them across Europe at a great profit. Its shipyard, called the Arsenal, could build ships very quickly, almost like a factory.

Portugal wanted to reach the spices by sea, so its captains sailed a little farther down the coast of Africa each year. In 1488 Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip, which was later named the Cape of Good Hope.
European merchants wanted to buy spices without paying the many traders in between. In 1498, the Portuguese captain Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa and reached Calicut in India.

A pilot who knew the monsoon guided Gama's ships across the ocean from East Africa to Calicut. The local ruler was not impressed by his cheap gifts, but Gama still carried home spices worth many times the cost of the voyage.

The Indian Ocean had long been open to everyone, but the Portuguese changed that by using armed ships. They seized ports such as Goa in 1510 and Malacca in 1511, and they forced other merchants to buy permits.
Lisbon soon became a great market for spices, and Portugal grew rich. Venice kept trading, however, and the old routes through Egypt did not disappear overnight.
Christopher Columbus believed that Asia lay only a short way to the west across the Atlantic. After years of asking, he persuaded Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand of Spain to pay for his ships.
In 1492, Christopher Columbus sailed west from Spain, hoping to reach Asia by a shorter way. Instead he reached islands in the Caribbean, and Europe's contact with the Americas began.

In October 1492 Columbus landed on a small island in the Bahamas, where he met the Taíno people. He thought that he had reached the Indies, so he called them Indians, and the mistake has lasted ever since.

Ships carried plants and animals across the oceans as well as people and goods. Potatoes, maize and tomatoes went from the Americas to the world, while wheat, horses and sugar cane travelled the other way.
The potato grew well in cold, stony ground where wheat struggled, and it fed millions of people in Europe. Maize and sweet potatoes did the same in parts of Africa and China.
The ships also carried diseases such as smallpox and measles, which the people of the Americas had never met before. Estimates vary, but in many regions most of the population died within a century.

In 1519 five ships left Spain under Ferdinand Magellan to find a western way to the spices. Magellan was killed in the Philippines in 1521, and only one ship, with eighteen men, finished the first voyage around the world in 1522.
From 1565, Spanish ships called galleons sailed regularly across the Pacific between Mexico and Manila. They carried American silver to Asia, and they brought back Chinese silk and porcelain.
In the Andes, a mountain at Potosí, in what is now Bolivia, produced vast quantities of silver. Many Indigenous workers were forced to labour in the mines, and many died.

By about 1600, trade joined every continent where people lived. In Mexico City, wealthy families wore Chinese silk and ate from Chinese porcelain, while Chinese traders sold goods bought with American silver.
In southwest China, bricks of pressed tea were carried over high mountains to Tibet. In return, Tibetans sent horses, which China always needed, so the path became known as the Tea Horse Road.

Porters carried huge stacks of tea bricks on their backs, and some loads were said to weigh as much as the porter himself. They carried a T-shaped stick, which they used to rest the load without putting it down.
In the cold, thin air of Tibet, people drank tea mixed with butter and salt many times a day. It warmed them, gave them energy, and made the demand for tea from China almost endless.

The Chinese government wanted Tibetan horses for its armies, so it ran offices where tea could be swapped for horses. Officials set the price, which was often a very large amount of tea for one animal.
Mountain towns such as Lijiang grew rich because the tea caravans stopped there to rest and trade. Their old stone streets, once crowded with mules and porters, are still used by visitors today.

The Inca Empire of South America built about thirty thousand kilometres of roads through mountains and deserts. They had no wheeled carts, so people and llamas walked, and relay runners carried messages.
The Inca called their empire Tawantinsuyu, which means the land of the four quarters. Four main roads led out from the capital, Cusco, towards the four parts of the empire.
Along the Inca roads, small huts stood every few kilometres, and in each of them a young runner waited. When a messenger arrived and called out, the next runner took the message and sprinted off.
The Inca had no writing like ours, but they kept careful records. They tied coloured cords with knots, called quipus, and trained officials read them to count people, goods and taxes.

Inca engineers crossed deep gorges with bridges made of woven grass ropes, which they had to renew every year. At Q'eswachaka, in Peru, villagers still rebuild one such bridge each June in the traditional way.

The roads of history also carried some terrible cargoes, and we should not forget them. For many centuries, enslaved people were marched across the Sahara and shipped across the Indian Ocean and the Atlantic to be sold.

For many centuries caravans carried captives from West and Central Africa north across the Sahara to be sold. The desert crossing was hard, and many people died of thirst and exhaustion along the way.
On the East African coast, captives were put on ships bound for Arabia, Persia and India. The trade grew in the nineteenth century, and the great slave market on Zanzibar was closed only in 1873.

From the early 1500s, European ships began to carry enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to the Americas. Over about 350 years, historians estimate that roughly twelve million people were forced on to these ships.

The voyage across the Atlantic was called the Middle Passage. People were packed tightly in the holds of ships, and historians believe that more than a million of them died before the ships reached land.
In the Americas, enslaved people were forced to grow sugar, cotton, tobacco and coffee, and they were not paid. The profits made some merchants, planters and port cities in Europe very rich.

Enslaved people never accepted their situation, and they resisted by revolts, escapes and by founding hidden communities. In Haiti, a great revolution ended slavery, and in 1804 the country became a free republic.

Campaigners, including former slaves such as Olaudah Equiano, wrote books and gathered petitions. Britain banned the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in its empire from 1833, and the United States ended slavery in 1865.

In the United States, a secret network called the Underground Railroad helped thousands of enslaved people to escape to the northern states and Canada. A brave woman named Harriet Tubman escaped herself and then returned to guide about seventy others.

Today memorials around the world remember the people who were taken, and a United Nations project has studied the slave routes since 1994. At Ouidah, in Benin, a monument called the Door of No Return stands near the sea where captives were marched to the ships.

China's Grand Canal joined the Yangtze and the Yellow rivers and carried grain from the rich south to the north. The first great sections were finished about fourteen hundred years ago, and some of it is still in use.

The Erie Canal in the United States opened in 1825, and it linked the Great Lakes with the Hudson river and New York. Mules walking on the bank pulled the boats, and the cost of sending goods fell dramatically.

In 1825, the Stockton and Darlington Railway in England opened, with a steam locomotive pulling the trains. The Liverpool and Manchester Railway followed in 1830, and it was the first line to depend on steam power alone.
Steamships did not depend on the wind, and in 1838 the Great Western crossed the Atlantic in about fifteen days. A sailing ship might take twice as long, especially when sailing against the wind.

Before railways, every town kept its own local time, set by the sun. Trains needed timetables, so British railways adopted one standard time in the 1840s, and North American railways set up time zones in 1883.
India's first passenger railway opened in 1853, between Bombay and Thane. It grew into one of the world's largest rail networks, but British rulers built it mainly to carry troops and raw materials.

On 10 May 1869, at a place called Promontory Summit in Utah, the two halves of the first American railway from coast to coast met. A final golden spike was hammered in, and a journey that once took months now took about a week.

Many thousands of Chinese immigrants did the hardest and most dangerous work on the Central Pacific line, cutting tunnels through the snowy Sierra Nevada mountains. Yet they were left out of the famous photograph of the golden spike ceremony.

The Trans-Siberian Railway was built between 1891 and 1916, and it runs for more than nine thousand kilometres from Moscow to Vladivostok. A passenger takes about a week to cross a country that spans eleven time zones.
Railway stations became the new crossroads, and whole towns grew up where lines met. Chicago, in the United States, became a great centre because dozens of railways came together there.

The Suez Canal opened in 1869, after about ten years of digging by Egyptian workers under the French engineer Ferdinand de Lesseps. It joined the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea, and many workers died during the work.

The Suez Canal made the sea journey from London to India several thousand kilometres shorter, because ships no longer had to go around Africa. Steamers could use it easily, and the trade between Europe and Asia grew fast.

The Panama Canal opened in 1914, after the French had failed and the Americans had worked for about ten years. Tens of thousands of workers laboured on it, and thousands died, mostly from diseases such as yellow fever and malaria.
The Panama Canal works like a staircase made of water, with huge locks at each end. Each ship is lifted about twenty-six metres to a lake in the middle, and then lowered again on the other side.
In the twentieth century, cars and lorries filled the roads, and engineers built smooth tarmac highways for them. Towns changed shape, because people could now live far from where they worked.

In 1908 the American engineer Henry Ford began to sell the Model T, a simple, strong car. From 1913 his workers built it on a moving assembly line, which made it cheap enough for ordinary families to buy.

In 1956 the United States began to build the Interstate Highway System, which grew to more than 70,000 kilometres of fast roads. Many other countries built motorways too, and the old network of country lanes was joined by a new kind of road.

On 17 December 1903, on a beach at Kitty Hawk in North Carolina, the Wright brothers made the first powered flights. The first lasted only twelve seconds, but the fourth of the day lasted nearly a minute.
Aeroplanes have created a whole new set of invisible roads across the sky. A journey from Europe to Asia that once took many months now takes less than a day.
Airports have become the new crossroads, and a few giant hubs connect most of the world's cities. A traveller can reach almost any city on Earth with one or two changes of plane.

Before the 1950s, dock workers loaded ships piece by piece, with every barrel, sack and crate handled many times. A trucking owner named Malcolm McLean saw that this was slow and wasteful, and he looked for a better way.
In 1956, a ship in the United States carried the first load of standard metal containers. Because the boxes could be lifted straight from ship to train to truck, shipping became much cheaper.
The key was standard sizes, so the same box fitted a ship, a train and a lorry anywhere in the world. Cranes could move the boxes in minutes, and ports became much quicker and cheaper.
Today the largest container ships can carry more than twenty thousand boxes, and they are almost four hundred metres long. A few thousand such ships carry most of the world's goods across the oceans.
A single shirt may be made of cotton grown in one country and spun in another. Its buttons come from a third, it is sewn in a fourth, and it is shipped in a container to a shop in a fifth.

In 1844, Samuel Morse sent a message from Washington to Baltimore along a telegraph wire, using a code of short and long signals. The wires soon followed the railways, and news could travel faster than any train.

In 1858, the first telegraph cable across the Atlantic Ocean was laid, although it soon failed. Today, almost all the information that crosses the oceans, from emails to video calls, travels through cables on the sea floor.

Hundreds of undersea cables now cross the oceans, and each has to be repaired when something goes wrong. Ship anchors and fishing nets sometimes cut them, and special repair ships go out to lift the broken ends and join them again.

Many ordinary English words travelled to us along these old roads of trade. Sugar came from Sanskrit through Arabic, algebra comes from an Arabic book title, and coffee passed through Turkish before it reached English.
In many languages, tea is called chai, as in Russian, Turkish and Hindi. In others, such as English, French and German, it is some form of tea, and the two words came from different parts of China.
Cities that sat where roads and sea lanes met often grew rich, such as Venice, Samarkand and Istanbul. Places that were bypassed, however, could fade away when the trade moved elsewhere.

Singapore was founded as a British trading post in 1819, and it stands at the southern end of the Strait of Malacca. A large share of the world's sea trade passes through this narrow channel, and the city has become one of the busiest ports on Earth.
Roads rise and fall with empires, wars and new technology. As sea routes grew safer and cheaper, many caravan towns of Central Asia lost trade and slowly grew quiet.

In the Taklamakan, towns such as Niya and Loulan were abandoned when their rivers dried up or the trade moved away. The dry sand preserved wooden houses, letters and tools, which archaeologists began to dig up in the early twentieth century.

In 2014, the United Nations cultural agency listed a stretch of the old Silk Road as a World Heritage Site. It includes 33 places in China, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, among them cities, temples, forts and tombs.

Some old roads are alive again, because ordinary people now walk them for pleasure or faith. The Camino de Santiago, a thousand-year-old pilgrim path across northern Spain, is walked by hundreds of thousands of people each year.
Roads have carried gifts and harms alike, and some have served certain people far better than others. Along them came medicines, crops and ideas, but also plagues, armies and slave traders.
Look carefully at the road that runs outside your own home. It may follow a path that people walked a thousand years ago, and it joins, step by step, the very roads in this story.
New roads are still being made today: more cables on the sea floor, satellites in the sky and fast trains across continents. As Arctic ice melts, ships may even open new sea routes in the far north.

Every road in this book began with a person who wanted something from far away, or wanted to see what lay beyond the hill. The next roads are still being made, and we are the ones who will travel them.
C1C2: At Laetoli, in Tanzania, a trail of footprints lies preserved in volcanic ash that hardened more than three million years ago. They were made by early members of the human family, walking upright across a plain still damp from a shower of rain. Every road in this book began in the same way, as the marks left by living feet that happened to go the same way.

In the 1970s, a team led by the scientist Mary Leakey uncovered the trail at Laetoli, a line of prints about twenty-seven metres long. It was made by two or three individuals, some smaller and some larger, who walked close together towards the north. Their steps are so clear that scientists can estimate how tall they were, how they stood and even how fast they moved.

Some three and a half million years ago, a volcano near Laetoli spread a layer of fine ash across the plain, and a shower of rain turned the surface into something like soft cement. Across that damp ground walked our distant relatives, pressing every step deep into the grey mud as they went. Soon the sun had baked the surface hard, and the next fall of ash sealed the prints under a protective blanket that kept them safe for ages.

The first roads were probably not made by people at all, but by animals that went back to the same river, salt lick or grazing ground day after day. Their hooves pressed the soil hard and wore the plants away, leaving a narrow, firm line that was easier to walk along than the bushes on either side. Hunters and gatherers who followed those tracks were simply taking the advice of creatures that had already worked out the shortest way.

The great migration out of Africa was not a single march but a slow drift, as small bands of modern humans moved into new country a few kilometres at a time. Over many thousands of years they followed river valleys and coastlines into Asia, Europe and eventually Australia, and they reached the Americas at least fifteen thousand years ago. Wherever they went, they carried tools, languages and stories, so every path across a continent was also a path for ideas.

Long before towns, coins or kings, people were already trading, for good tools were worth a long walk. Obsidian, a black volcanic glass that can be flaked into razor-sharp blades, was carried hundreds of kilometres from the few mountains where it was found. Such journeys, repeated over many centuries by countless travellers, wore the first lasting tracks across the land.

Archaeologists have dug up beads made from sea shells at camps and graves hundreds of kilometres from the nearest coast. Such small ornaments were probably passed from group to group as gifts, as marks of friendship or as payment, long before anyone had invented money. Every bead of this kind is a tiny piece of evidence that people who never saw the sea could still reach it through their friends.

In 1991, two hikers noticed a body lying in the melting ice of the Alps, on the border between Italy and Austria, and it proved to be about 5,300 years old. The man, now known as Ötzi, wore clothes of leather and grass, carried a bow and a copper axe, and owned flint tools made from stone that came from other valleys. His belongings show that people of that age already moved through high mountains and used goods that had travelled far.

One of the oldest boats ever discovered is a canoe found at Pesse, in the Netherlands, which was hollowed out of a single pine trunk about ten thousand years ago. Boats like this let hunters, fishermen and traders cross lakes and follow rivers into country that was too thick with forest or marsh to cross on foot. For much of history, water was easier and cheaper to travel than land, and that fact will return again and again in this story.

Nobody designs a path; it appears when one person finds a good way across the land and others decide to trust that judgement. Each pair of feet presses the soil a little harder and wears away a little more grass, until the line is clear enough for a stranger to follow in the dark. Once a path is trusted, villages grow beside it, merchants rely on it, and rulers begin to wonder how they might tax it.

In ancient Egypt, the great river Nile was the country's main road, and almost everyone lived within sight of its banks. The current carried boats northward with little effort, while the wind, which usually blows from the north, allowed sailors to raise their sails and travel back against it. Few lands have ever been so neatly designed for the movement of heavy goods.
