About 4,500 years ago, an inspector named Merer led a crew of boatmen who carried blocks of white limestone down the Nile to the Great Pyramid at Giza. He kept a logbook on papyrus, noting where the boats stopped and what was loaded each day, and the rolls were found in 2013 at an ancient harbour beside the Red Sea. They are among the oldest inscribed papyri ever discovered, and they read like the diary of a modern delivery driver.

About 1470 BCE the Egyptian queen Hatshepsut sent five ships down the Red Sea to a land called Punt, whose exact position scholars still debate. The sailors returned with gold, ivory, ebony and living incense trees in baskets, and the queen had the whole voyage carved in pictures on the walls of her great temple at Deir el-Bahari. It is one of the earliest trading voyages for which we have such a detailed picture.

Wheeled vehicles appeared in several parts of Eurasia more than five thousand years ago, and they changed what a road had to be. A footpath was good enough for a walker or a donkey, but a heavy cart needed a wide, firm and fairly level surface, and that meant organised labour. Building and mending roads, in other words, quickly became one of the most important jobs of any government.

Donkeys were tamed from the wild ass in northeast Africa more than five thousand years ago, and for a long time they were the most important carriers of freight on land. A donkey is sure-footed on stony slopes, content with poor grazing and strong enough to carry a heavy load for many days. Without this patient animal, most of the early caravans of the ancient world could not have crossed the mountains.

About four thousand years ago, merchants from the city of Assur in what is now Iraq sent caravans of donkeys loaded with tin and woollen cloth to trading towns in Anatolia, in modern Turkey. We know this in remarkable detail because the traders wrote their letters and accounts on clay tablets, and thousands of them have been dug up at a site called Kanesh. They complain about taxes, bandits and late payments in a way that any modern businessperson would recognise.

Some of the best letters were written by women, for the trade was a family business. Wives and sisters in Assur wove woollen cloth at home, packed it for the caravans and then wrote to their men in Anatolia, asking for silver and scolding them for slow replies. Across four thousand years, we can still hear the voices of people who were never kings or generals.

Bronze, the great metal of the ancient world, is a mixture of copper with a small amount of tin, and it is harder and more useful than copper alone. Copper was found in many places, but tin was scarce, so rulers who wanted bronze weapons and tools had to buy it from distant merchants. A metal that was cheap in one valley could therefore be worth a fortune in another, and that difference is the secret engine of nearly all long-distance trade.

About 3,300 years ago a merchant ship went down off the southern coast of Turkey, near a place now called Uluburun, and lay undisturbed on the seabed until a sponge diver found it in 1982. Archaeologists later raised about ten tonnes of copper ingots, together with tin, blue glass, ebony, ivory and jewellery that had been gathered from places hundreds or even thousands of kilometres apart. The wreck is a time capsule that shows how far the trade of the Bronze Age reached.

Long before the Silk Road had a name, the cities of the Indus valley, in what is now Pakistan and India, were sending goods towards Mesopotamia, probably by ship around the coast of Arabia. Their merchants carried small stone seals carved with animals and with signs that nobody can yet read, and some of those seals have turned up in the ruins of Mesopotamian cities. Mesopotamian texts also mention a distant land called Meluhha, which many scholars believe was the Indus region.

The camel is the perfect desert traveller, and its body seems to have been designed for dry country. Its broad, soft feet spread out on loose sand, its double rows of eyelashes keep out the blowing dust, and its hump stores fat that the animal can use as food when there is nothing to eat. A well-fed camel can cross a great waste for days at a time, carrying a load that would exhaust a horse.

Frankincense is the hardened sap of trees that grow in the dry hills of southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa. Harvesters cut the bark with a sharp tool, and the milky liquid that oozed out dried slowly into pale, fragrant tears which could be gathered a few weeks later. When they were burned on hot coals, they gave off the sweet smoke that people in many lands offered to their gods.

In southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa grew trees whose sticky resins, frankincense and myrrh, were burned in temples and palaces across the ancient world. Camels, which had been tamed as pack animals by about three thousand years ago, carried them north through the desert along a chain of wells and oasis towns. Whoever controlled a well on that route could grow rich simply by providing water.

Across the ancient world, fragrant smoke was a way of speaking to the gods, and temples, palaces and funerals all needed a steady supply. Incense was also used as perfume, as a medicine and as a gift fit for a king. Since the trees grew in just a few regions, the demand of a hundred distant cities was met by a thin and expensive stream of caravans.

The Nabataeans, an Arab people of the desert, built the astonishing city of Petra in the rocky country of what is now Jordan, with temples and tombs carved straight into the pink cliffs. Their wealth came from the caravans, for they knew where every well was hidden and they charged merchants for water, guides and protection. A people who might have remained desert wanderers became rich by understanding a single fact, which is that travellers need to drink.

By about 500 BCE the Persian Empire reached from Egypt and Turkey in the west to the borders of India in the east, and it was the largest state that the world had yet seen. A king in his palace needed to know what was happening in every province, and the provinces needed to hear his orders. Government on that scale was impossible without roads, and the Persians became some of the best road managers in history.

Around two and a half thousand years ago, the kings of Persia kept up a great highway, the Royal Road, which ran for some two thousand five hundred kilometres from Sardis to Susa. Along it stood stations with fresh horses and rest houses, so that a message could be passed from rider to rider without a pause. The Greek writer Herodotus admired these couriers, and their service has often been called the ancient ancestor of the postal system.

About 500 BCE the Persian king Darius completed a canal that joined the Nile to the Red Sea, a task that earlier Egyptian rulers had begun but never finished. He had the achievement recorded on stone monuments, which say that ships carrying tribute sailed through it from Egypt to Persia. More than two thousand years before the Suez Canal, a ruler had already seen how much a short cut across a narrow strip of land was worth.

About 600 BCE the kingdom of Lydia, whose capital Sardis lay at the western end of the Royal Road, began to stamp lumps of a natural gold and silver mixture with a royal sign. A coin was easy to carry, easy to count and guaranteed by a ruler, so it was far more convenient for a merchant than a sack of grain or a bar of silver that had to be weighed. Money did not create trade, but it made trade over long distances much easier.

The Phoenicians, who lived along the coast of what is now Lebanon, were the great sailors of the early Mediterranean, and their ships carried cloth dyed purple, glass, timber and metal to ports from Spain to Egypt. They also carried a simple alphabet of about twenty-two letters, which was far easier to learn than older systems of writing. That handful of symbols, passed from trader to trader, became the ancestor of the Greek and Latin letters, and of many others.

Alexander became king of Macedonia in 336 BCE, when his father was murdered and the young man was only twenty years old. Within two years he had led an army of Macedonians and Greeks across the narrow sea into Asia, determined to challenge the mighty Persian Empire. It was a bold gamble, for Persia had armies and treasure that seemed to be beyond any rival's reach.

In 331 BCE Alexander founded a new city on the Mediterranean coast of Egypt and, characteristically, gave it his own name. Alexandria grew into one of the greatest ports of the ancient world, with a towering lighthouse, a great library and merchants from Greece, Egypt, Arabia and India. Of all the cities that bore his name, it was the one that truly fulfilled his hopes.

Having beaten the Persian king and seized his great palaces, Alexander pressed on eastwards and led his army over the snowy peaks of the Hindu Kush into Bactria, in what is now Afghanistan. The crossing cost him many men, who suffered from cold, hunger and the thin mountain air. In 327 BCE he married Roxana, the daughter of a local nobleman, in the hope of making peace between the conquerors and the conquered.

Beside the Syr Darya river, on the far edge of Central Asia, Alexander founded around 329 BCE a city called Alexandria Eschate, a name that meant Alexandria the Farthest. He settled wounded soldiers and local people there, and ancient writers say that his builders raised the walls in about twenty days. The new town was meant to be both a fortress against the nomads and a market where two worlds could meet.

In 326 BCE Alexander led his army through the passes of the Hindu Kush and into northern India, where he won a hard battle against a king named Porus. At the next great river, after eight years of marching and fighting, his exhausted soldiers refused to go any farther. For the first time, the conqueror gave way, and the army turned back towards the west.

In Gandhara, a region that now lies in Pakistan and Afghanistan, sculptors carved Buddhist figures in a style that borrowed boldly from Greece. Their stone Buddhas wear heavy folded robes and have wavy hair, and they look remarkably like Greek statues of gods and heroes. It is a fine example of how a road can carry an artistic idea in one direction and a religious idea in the other, until the two become one thing.

After Alexander's death in 323 BCE, his empire fell apart, but Greek kings kept control of Bactria and, later, of parts of northern India for about two hundred years. They struck handsome silver coins that bore their portraits and Greek words, and many of these coins still turn up in the soil of Afghanistan. For two centuries, then, a Greek-speaking court sat in the middle of Asia, close to the roads that would later carry silk.

Around 250 BCE the Indian emperor Ashoka, who ruled most of the subcontinent, announced on stone pillars that he had planted shade trees and dug wells along the roads for the use of people and animals. He also built rest houses at intervals, so that a traveller might find water and a bed at the end of the day. A ruler who cares for the road, he understood, is caring for the whole country that it joins.

Ashoka became a follower of the Buddha, and he sent teachers and messengers to distant lands, including the island now called Sri Lanka and the Greek kingdoms of the west. Over the next centuries, monks and merchants travelled together, for the monks needed safe passage and protection, and the merchants were glad to give gifts to holy men. In this way one man's change of heart began a movement of ideas that would reach all the way to Japan.

Alexander died in Babylon in 323 BCE at the age of thirty-two, after a short illness, and his generals quickly began to quarrel over the pieces of his enormous empire. The empire itself did not last, but the cities, the roads and the Greek-speaking merchants that it had created stayed in place. He had been a conqueror, but his most lasting gift to history was a set of connections.

By about 140 BCE the Han Empire was large, rich and well governed, yet it had a persistent problem on its northern frontier. The Xiongnu, a confederation of nomads who lived on the grasslands, could fire arrows from the backs of galloping horses and vanish before an army arrived. The emperor Wu, who had come to the throne young and ambitious, was determined to find a better answer.

The emperor learned that a people called the Yuezhi, whom the Xiongnu had driven from the borders of China, had settled far away to the west and still hated their old enemy. About 138 BCE he chose an officer named Zhang Qian to lead a party of about a hundred men to find them and propose an alliance. Nobody at court could say how far the journey was, for no Chinese official had ever travelled so far to the west.

Zhang Qian had barely crossed the frontier when Xiongnu horsemen captured him, and they held him prisoner for about ten years. He was given a wife and had a son, yet he kept the staff that marked him as the emperor's envoy and secretly kept his mission alive. One day, when the guards had grown careless, he and a few companions slipped away to the west.

After his escape, Zhang Qian travelled west for many weeks, crossed the mountains of the Pamir and arrived in Ferghana, a green valley of walled towns, vineyards and fine horses. The people there treated him kindly and sent him on to the Yuezhi, who had settled in Bactria and had no wish to fight again. He took careful note of everything that he saw, from the shape of the towns to the way the people farmed.

In the bazaars of Bactria, Zhang Qian was astonished to find bamboo canes and fine cloth that he recognised as products of his own country's southwest. The merchants explained that these goods had reached them through India, which meant that a route between China and the west already existed, unknown to the imperial court. His report taught the emperor that the world was larger and better connected than anyone in the capital had imagined.

On the journey home Zhang Qian was captured once more by the Xiongnu, but a quarrel among them gave him the chance to escape, and he reached the Han capital after thirteen years away. Of the hundred or so men who had set out with him, only he and one companion returned. The emperor, who had probably given him up for dead, rewarded him with high office and listened carefully to his tales.

In the valley of Ferghana, Zhang had seen powerful horses that the Chinese later called heavenly horses, and the Han court wanted them for its cavalry. China could offer silk in exchange, a fabric that the rest of the world still could not make. Gradually, a trickle of silk heading west and horses heading east grew into a steady flow.

When the king of Ferghana refused to hand over his finest horses, the Han emperor sent an army across the deserts to take them by force. The first expedition failed disastrously, with many of the men lost to thirst and hunger, but a second, much larger army besieged the capital in about 101 BCE. The defeated people agreed to supply a great number of horses, and China's western frontier was suddenly much farther from the capital than before.

To protect the new routes, the Han government extended its walls of packed earth and its lines of watchtowers far into the western desert, as far as Dunhuang. Soldiers on the towers lit fires or smoke signals when raiders approached, so that a warning could cross hundreds of kilometres much faster than any rider. The same garrisons also checked the papers of merchants and travellers, and their stations became the first customs posts on the road.

West of Dunhuang stood a fortified pass known as the Jade Gate, a name that recalled the precious green stone that entered China there from the western oases. For a traveller leaving the empire, it was the last place where officials and soldiers could be relied upon to help. Beyond it lay the dry basin of the Taklamakan, and the road that Zhang Qian had opened now began.

The silkworm is the caterpillar of a small moth, and it feeds greedily on the leaves of the mulberry tree until it is ready to spin. It then wraps itself in a cocoon made from one continuous thread that may be several hundred metres long. To make cloth, the farmers had to unwind the thread without breaking it, and that delicate craft took years to learn.

Silk was so valuable in Han China that the government treated it almost as a second currency, paying soldiers and officials with rolls of it and accepting it in taxes. It also sent enormous gifts of silk to the Xiongnu leaders, hoping that costly presents would be cheaper than war. Some of the silk that reached the west therefore began its journey as a bribe, a salary or a peace offering.

By the first century CE, wealthy Romans prized silk for its softness and for its shimmer, and the thinnest cloths were considered scandalous. Writers such as Pliny the Elder grumbled that the empire was losing enormous sums of money every year to the distant lands that sold it such luxuries. Complaints about the cost of fashion have a very long history, and this one is nearly two thousand years old.

The name Silk Road is surprisingly recent, for it was coined in 1877 by a German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen, long after the caravans had stopped. In reality there was never a single road but a shifting web of tracks, passes and sea lanes, which changed with the seasons, the weather and the politics of the day. Even the name, then, is a little misleading, but it has stuck because it captures a very large idea well.

Merchants never tried to cross the middle of the Taklamakan desert, for the shifting dunes offered no water and no shade. Instead, caravans followed one of two main branches that curved around it, a northern one along the foot of the Tian Shan mountains and a southern one beside the Kunlun mountains. Both routes passed through a chain of oasis towns, and both met again in the far west at Kashgar.

The Taklamakan desert, a sea of shifting dunes, and the high passes of the Pamir mountains tested every caravan. Few merchants travelled the whole distance; most took their goods a single stretch of the journey and sold them on to the next trader, so that a bale of silk might change hands a dozen times. Prices rose with every handover, and by the time the cloth reached Rome it cost many times what it had cost in China.

Wherever springs or rivers made life possible in the dry heart of Asia, oasis cities such as Samarkand, Kashgar and Dunhuang grew rich as meeting places for merchants. Their bazaars offered silk, spices, glass, horses, jade and gossip from a dozen countries, all haggled over in several languages. The hardy, two-humped Bactrian camel, which tolerates both fierce heat and bitter cold, carried much of the freight.

Between about 300 and 700 CE, much of the trade across Central Asia was in the hands of the Sogdians, a people whose homeland lay around Samarkand. They founded trading communities all the way to the cities of China, spoke several languages, and wrote letters that were sealed and carried by relays of travellers. Their language was widely used as a common tongue of the road for several centuries.

Around 313 CE, a Sogdian woman named Miwnay, who had been left in the Chinese town of Dunhuang with her daughter, wrote an angry and desperate letter to her husband in Samarkand. The letter, which was sealed in a bundle and never delivered, was found in a ruined watchtower in 1907, and in it she begs him to send money and help. Behind the great trade of the Silk Road we hear a very human voice, and it sounds like a family in trouble.

In 97 CE a Chinese envoy named Gan Ying travelled to the shores of the sea beyond Parthia, hoping to go on to Rome. Local sailors warned him that the voyage might take two years and that many travellers fell sick with longing for home, so he turned back. Chinese records report that, in 166 CE, men claiming to be envoys of the Roman emperor arrived at the Han court by sea, though they were probably merchants.

At its height, the Roman Empire was crossed by tens of thousands of kilometres of paved roads, laid in layers of gravel and stone with ditches at the sides to carry off the rain. They were built so that soldiers could march quickly to any trouble, yet they were soon crowded with merchants, messengers and pilgrims. Milestones along the way told every traveller how far it was to the next town.

The Appian Way, begun in 312 BCE by a Roman official named Appius Claudius, ran south from Rome and was later extended to the port of Brindisi, from which ships sailed to Greece and the East. Its great paving stones fit together so closely that stretches of the road can still be walked, and they earned it the Roman title of queen of roads. Tombs and monuments lined its edges, so travellers passed a long procession of the dead on their way out of the city.

The first emperor, Augustus, set up an imperial post called the cursus publicus, in which stations at regular distances along the main roads kept fresh horses, carriages and rooms for officials. Urgent news could therefore travel many times faster than a walker could carry it, and the emperor could keep a firm hand on provinces thousands of kilometres away. The system was reserved for the government, but the same roads, bridges and inns were open to everybody.

Rome, which by the first century CE may have held a million people, could not feed itself from the farmland around it. Great grain ships, some of them able to carry more than a thousand tonnes according to ancient writers, brought wheat from Egypt and North Africa to the port of Ostia, and the emperors made sure that the supply never failed. The capital of the world lived, in other words, on a sea road as much as on its famous stone ones.

In the Indian Ocean the great winds called monsoons reverse direction with the seasons, blowing from the southwest in summer and from the northeast in winter. Sailors learned to ride them like a ferry timetable, sailing east to India when the summer wind blew and returning west when it turned. A Greek-speaking merchant of the first century wrote a guide to these ports, called the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, which still survives.

Ships that had crossed from India unloaded their cargoes at Red Sea ports such as Berenike, whose ruins have been dug up by archaeologists who found pepper, beads and Indian pottery in them. From there, long camel trains plodded for many days across the stony eastern desert to the Nile, and boats carried the goods down to Alexandria. A bag of pepper bought on the coast of India therefore crossed an ocean, a desert and a river before it reached a Roman kitchen.

Black pepper, which grows on a climbing vine in southern India, was one of the most sought-after spices in the Roman world, and cooks used it in the grandest dishes. Hoards of Roman gold and silver coins have been dug up in southern India, which suggests how much money flowed east to pay for it. Spices, in other words, were small things that moved a very large amount of wealth.

A broken papyrus of the second century CE, now kept in Vienna, records the cargo of a merchant ship called the Hermapollon, which had sailed from the Indian port of Muziris to Egypt. It lists valuable goods such as ivory, scented oils and textiles, and scholars who have worked out its value believe that it could have bought a large estate in Italy. One sheet of old paper tells us more about the scale of the sea trade than a library of poems.

In the 1930s, French archaeologists at Begram, in Afghanistan, opened two sealed rooms in an ancient palace and found a treasure that nobody had expected. There were bowls of Roman glass, carved ivory plaques from India and Chinese lacquer boxes, all about two thousand years old, as if the shopping of three empires had been stored side by side. Begram sat where the roads crossed, and the rooms show the fact better than any map.

Palmyra, an oasis city in the Syrian desert, grew rich as a rest stop for caravans carrying silk, spices and perfume from the east towards the Roman Empire. A stone tablet of 137 CE sets out the taxes on each kind of goods, from oil to dyed wool, and it shows that the city was run by sensible and businesslike people. Its queen Zenobia later challenged Rome, but she was defeated in 272 CE, and the city never recovered its glory.

In 148 CE a Parthian monk named An Shigao arrived in the Chinese capital, Luoyang, having travelled thousands of kilometres from the far west. He learned Chinese and spent more than twenty years translating Buddhist texts, which were then copied and passed from hand to hand. Like many of the first teachers, he was a foreigner, and his work shows that the road carried teachers as well as traders.

Kumarajiva was born in the oasis kingdom of Kucha, on the northern branch of the Silk Road, and he mastered Sanskrit and several other languages as a young man. In 401 CE he was brought to the Chinese capital, where he led a large team that turned many Buddhist works into smooth and elegant Chinese. Because their translations read so well, many of them are still recited in East Asia today.

Around 399 CE a Chinese monk named Faxian, who was already past sixty according to tradition, set out on foot to look for the original rules and texts of his faith in India. He crossed the dreaded Taklamakan and the high mountain passes, spent years studying and copying, and finally sailed home across the ocean on a merchant ship. His account of the journey is one of the earliest travel books written by a Chinese author, and it is full of dangers and wonders.

Buddhism travelled out of India with merchants and monks, spread through the oasis towns of Central Asia, and reached China, where the cave temples of Dunhuang still glow with painted walls. In 629 CE, a Chinese monk named Xuanzang set out, largely on foot, to study at the sources of the faith in India, and he returned sixteen years later with hundreds of texts. His journey, together with his detailed account of what he saw, is one of the great travel stories of the ancient world.

On his return to China, Xuanzang wrote a detailed account of the kingdoms, customs, cities and climates that he had passed through, and historians still rely on it as one of the best descriptions of the Asia of his day. Nearly a thousand years later, a novelist used the journey as the starting point for the adventure story known as Journey to the West, in which a monk is protected by a monkey king. The real traveller, who had nothing but his courage and his faith, was in some ways more remarkable than the monkey.

In the north of India stood Nalanda, a great monastery that worked like a university, with libraries, lecture halls and thousands of students and teachers. Xuanzang studied there for some years, and scholars came to it from China, Korea, Tibet, Indonesia and many other lands, so the roads that led to it were full of young people carrying notebooks. Few places in the ancient world were so devoted to learning for its own sake.

Near Dunhuang, in a long cliff above a dry riverbed, a monk began to carve a cave temple in about 366 CE, and over the next thousand years others added hundreds more. Merchants who were about to enter the dangerous desert paid for paintings in the hope of a safe journey, and the walls now glow with Buddhas, flying musicians, camel trains and scenes of everyday life. These are the Mogao caves, and they are like a picture album of the Silk Road.

In 1900 a Daoist priest named Wang Yuanlu, who was cleaning a cave at Mogao, noticed a hidden doorway behind a painted wall, and behind it he found a small room packed with tens of thousands of scrolls. They had been sealed up about a thousand years earlier, and they were written in Chinese, Tibetan, Sogdian and many other languages. Among them was a printed copy of the Diamond Sutra, dated 868, which is the oldest dated printed book in the world.

Goods were never the only cargo on the roads, for beliefs, stories and philosophies travelled with the merchants. Buddhism, Christianity, Islam and the teachings of a Persian prophet named Mani all spread along the routes of Asia at different times. In a few busy towns, their followers worshipped within sight of one another and learned, often with difficulty, to live as neighbours.

Chinese workers made paper by beating old rags, bark and plant fibres into a wet pulp, which they spread thinly on a fine screen and left to dry in the sun. A court official named Cai Lun is traditionally credited with improving the process in about 105 CE, although archaeologists have found even older scraps. Compared with bamboo strips or rolls of silk, the new material was cheap, light and easy to write on.

For centuries China kept the craft of papermaking to itself, but a secret that depends on a few skilled workers can never be guarded for ever. A popular story says that Chinese prisoners taught the art to their captors after a battle beside the Talas river in 751, and although historians doubt the details, it is certain that a paper mill was working in Samarkand soon afterwards. The craft had crossed the mountains, and the Islamic world was about to put it to remarkable use.

The city of Baghdad, founded in 762 on the banks of the Tigris, soon became a crossroads of trade and learning, where caravans and river boats met. Scholars working there translated books from Greek, Persian, Sanskrit and Syriac into Arabic and then added discoveries of their own in mathematics, medicine and astronomy. Many of those ideas later passed on to Europe, which owed a great deal to this meeting of cultures.

Paper was far cheaper than parchment, which had to be made from animal skin, and far easier to write on than a papyrus roll that cracked with age. By about 800 a paper mill was working in Baghdad, and writers of the time describe whole streets of booksellers, as well as copyists who earned their living by making new editions. A city that could produce books in such numbers soon had more readers than any in Europe.

Under the caliph al-Ma'mun, teams of astronomers from Baghdad went out into the Syrian desert about the year 830, measured the angle of the sun at two places and used the difference to calculate the size of the Earth. Scholars still debate the exact units that they used, but their result seems to have been remarkably close to the truth. The Earth, they knew perfectly well, was round, and the roads that crossed it were curves on a ball.

Al-Khwarizmi, who worked in Baghdad in the early ninth century, wrote a famous book explaining how to calculate with the Indian system of numbers, including the humble circle that stood for zero. When his work was translated into Latin hundreds of years later, European scholars learned a method far easier than Roman numerals, and his name, in its Latin form, gave us the word algorithm. A handful of symbols that had been invented in India travelled through Baghdad and changed arithmetic everywhere.

Around the year 700, the Tang capital of Chang'an was probably one of the largest cities on Earth, with a population that may have approached a million. Its wide avenues, laid out in a tidy grid, were thronged with traders, envoys and students from Persia, India, Korea and Japan. A visitor could hear a dozen languages in an afternoon and buy goods from three continents.

Chang'an was planned like a chessboard, with straight avenues crossing at right angles and the city divided into more than a hundred walled neighbourhoods, whose gates were shut at night. Two great markets, one in the east and one in the west, opened at midday to the sound of a drum and closed again before sunset, so that every transaction could be supervised. The Western Market, where the foreign merchants gathered, was the busier and more colourful of the two.

The Tang court was fascinated by everything foreign, and the fashion for Persian and Central Asian styles spread through the capital. People wore tight-sleeved coats and pointed boots, listened to the music of Central Asian lutes and watched Sogdian dancers who spun like tops, while polo, a game from Persia, became a passion at court, even among noblewomen. Tomb figures of the time show Sogdian merchants and their camels with such lively detail that we can almost hear the bells.

In 755 a powerful general named An Lushan, whose family came from the peoples of the northern frontier and who had Sogdian and Turkic connections, rose in revolt against the Tang emperor. The rebellion lasted for about eight years and cost millions of lives, and the government pulled its garrisons back from the west to defend its heartland. Tibetan armies soon occupied much of the oasis country, and the great overland road passed out of China's care.

Around 830 CE a sewn-plank ship of Arab design, bound for the Persian Gulf, sank off the island of Belitung in Indonesia with a cargo that had been loaded in China. Fishermen found it in 1998, and divers brought up about 60,000 pieces of Chinese pottery, together with gold and silver objects, in a haul that astonished the experts. The wreck shows that, while the overland road was fading, the sea road was already carrying goods in huge quantities.

Across the Sahara, caravans of camels carried salt, copper and cloth south to West Africa and returned with gold, ivory and kola nuts. The great empires that arose south of the desert, Ghana and later Mali, grew strong partly by taxing and protecting this trade. Salt, which was scarce in the forest and grassland, was sometimes said to be worth its weight in gold.

Before the camel arrived, crossing the Sahara was almost impossible, for horses and oxen needed far more water than the wells of the desert could provide. Camels reached North Africa in the first centuries CE, and over the following hundreds of years traders learned to organise them into large and regular caravans. The desert, which had been a wall, began to look like a sea that could be sailed with the right ships.

At Taghaza, a mining settlement in the middle of the Sahara, workers dug great slabs of salt out of the ground and loaded them on camels, two slabs to each animal. The traveller Ibn Battuta, who passed through in 1352, reported that the houses and even the mosque were built of salt blocks and roofed with camel skins, and he did not enjoy his stay. Nobody lived there for pleasure, and the miners depended on caravans to bring them every other necessity.

The gold of West Africa came from river gravel and shallow pits in the wooded country far to the south of the desert, where miners and panners worked it out by hand. Traders carried it north across the Sahara in small, heavy bags, and historians believe that a large part of the gold used for coins in the medieval Middle East and Europe came from this source. A king who controlled the road had a very strong card to play in his dealings with the rest of the world.

The empire of Ghana, which lay far to the north-west of the modern country that has taken its name, was a strong and wealthy state by about the year 1000. Its kings did not own the gold fields, but they taxed the traders who carried gold and salt through their territory, and they kept an army large enough to make sure that they were paid. Arab writers described the ruler's court as one of the richest in the world.

Muslim merchants from North Africa brought their religion and the Arabic language along the caravan roads, and over the centuries many West African rulers, scholars and traders accepted Islam. In the trading towns, they built mosques of mud brick strengthened with wooden beams, and schools where children learned to read and write in Arabic. In this way faith, like salt and gold, was carried across the desert by camel.

About 1235 a ruler named Sundiata Keita defeated the king of a rival state and founded the empire of Mali, which soon controlled the gold fields and the roads to the north. His life became an epic that West African storytellers, called griots, have recited for hundreds of years, and which is partly history and partly legend. In a world without printed books, such living memories kept the story of a nation alive.

In 1324 Mansa Musa, the ruler of the empire of Mali, set out on a pilgrimage to Mecca with a vast following, a large part of it carrying gold. In Cairo he gave away so much of it, according to writers of the time, that the price of gold there fell and stayed low for years. Later he brought scholars and builders home, and the city of Timbuktu became a famous centre of learning.

Timbuktu stood where the Sahara met the great bend of the Niger river, and it became a meeting place for camel caravans and river boats. Its mosques and schools drew scholars who studied law, medicine, mathematics and astronomy, and a visitor in the sixteenth century wrote that books brought more profit there than any other merchandise. A town built of mud had become a capital of the mind, known to scholars across the Muslim world.

Tens of thousands of manuscripts from Timbuktu have survived, and some estimates run far higher, because families hid them in chests and cellars and passed them from one generation to the next. In 2012, when armed fighters occupied the city, librarians and neighbours secretly packed many of the books and sent them south in boxes, by car and by boat. These readers saved a part of the world's memory with nothing more than courage and a great many wooden chests.

Arab, Indian and African sailors crossed the Indian Ocean in dhows, graceful wooden ships whose triangular sails could be set at a slant to catch the wind. Some of the early ones had planks stitched together with cord made from coconut fibre, a method that made them flexible enough to survive rough water and easy to repair. For centuries the monsoon and the dhow were the engine of a great trading world.

Along the coast of East Africa, a string of port towns, among them Kilwa, grew prosperous by shipping gold, ivory and timber across the Indian Ocean. Their people, the Swahili, spoke a language rooted in Africa but rich in words from Arabic, and they built mosques and houses of coral stone. Fragments of Chinese porcelain and Indian beads found in their ruins show how far their trade reached.

Far inland from the Swahili coast, in what is now the country of Zimbabwe, stood a great city of stone, whose curving walls still rise as high as eleven metres. It flourished from about 1100 to 1450, and its rulers grew rich from cattle and from gold that was shipped through the coastal ports. Archaeologists have found Chinese porcelain and glass beads among its ruins, and they show that even a city far from the sea belonged to the network.

In 1325 a young scholar named Ibn Battuta left his home in Tangier, in Morocco, intending only to make the pilgrimage to Mecca, but he found that he could not stop. He travelled for about thirty years through Africa, Arabia, Persia, India, Southeast Asia and probably China, covering some 120,000 kilometres, and he dictated an account that is one of the great travel books of the world. His book is full of marvels, and historians believe that he sometimes borrowed from other writers.

In the harbours of India, and at the Chinese port of Quanzhou, Ibn Battuta saw enormous Chinese ships with several decks and as many as twelve sails. He described cabins that had locks so that merchants could keep their goods safe, and he wrote that the biggest ships carried hundreds of men, with smaller boats towing them in and out of port. The Chinese were then the world's most skilful shipbuilders, and everyone who sailed the Indian Ocean knew it.

Chinese ships, known as junks, were built with watertight compartments inside the hull, so that a leak in one part would not sink the whole vessel. Their sails were stiffened with bamboo battens that could be adjusted in a moment, and by about the year 1100 Chinese sailors were also using the magnetic compass at sea, which let them keep their course in fog and cloud. Inventions of this kind later reached Arab and European sailors and changed the way that they sailed.

In 1405 the Ming emperor chose Zheng He, a Muslim official who had risen at court from a humble start, to lead a great fleet across the Indian Ocean. Chinese records say that it included more than two hundred ships and some 27,000 men, among them sailors, soldiers, doctors, interpreters and cooks. It was the largest naval expedition that the world had yet seen, and its purpose was to impress other rulers and to bring them into friendly relations with China.

Chinese records describe huge treasure ships with nine masts and a length of up to about 120 metres, and they claim that such a vessel was far larger than anything that Europeans would build for several centuries. Many historians believe that the real ships were somewhat smaller, but even the lower estimates make them enormous for their time. Whatever their exact size, they were certainly an impressive sight in any harbour of the Indian Ocean.

In 1414 a giraffe from Africa, which had been passed along the sea routes as a diplomatic gift, was presented to the Chinese emperor, and it caused a sensation. Courtiers compared the strange animal with the qilin, a gentle and lucky creature from ancient stories, and they took its arrival as a sign that the emperor ruled well. Artists painted it, and the picture survives to remind us how far a single present could travel.

Zheng He's seventh voyage ended in 1433, and the admiral himself probably died during it or soon afterwards, while the Chinese government turned its attention to its northern frontier and to the cost of its fleets. Historians still debate exactly why the voyages stopped, and some argue that private trade by sea carried on regardless. What is certain is that no Chinese admiral ever led such a fleet again, and the sea roads of the Indian Ocean lay open to newcomers.

The Mongols were herders who lived in felt tents on the wide grasslands of the steppe, and their children learned to ride almost before they could walk. In 1206, after years of fighting between rival clans, a leader named Temujin brought the tribes together and was proclaimed Genghis Khan, which is often translated as universal ruler. The united Mongols were a formidable force, for they were superb horsemen who could cover enormous distances with very little baggage.

In the thirteenth century the Mongols created the largest connected land empire in history, reaching from the Pacific coast of China to the borders of Eastern Europe. Their conquests were violent, and entire cities were destroyed, yet once their rule was established they made the routes through Central Asia safer than they had been for generations. Merchants who had once feared robbers found that a single government now protected the road from end to end.

Once the fighting was over, the Mongol rulers punished robbers severely and removed many of the local lords who had demanded payment from every passing caravan. Travellers could therefore go much farther at much lower risk, and it was said, no doubt with some exaggeration, that a person could carry a bag of gold across the whole empire and come to no harm. Historians sometimes call this period the Mongol peace, though it was a peace that rested on fear.

The Mongol rulers organised a vast relay system, called the yam, in which stations at regular intervals provided fresh horses, food and shelter for official messengers. A traveller with the right metal tablet, known as a paiza, could demand help along the whole route, and at its fastest a message might cover hundreds of kilometres in a single day. The network was designed for the government's use, but merchants and explorers benefited from it as well.

Karakorum, the Mongol capital, was a city of tents and wagons with a few grand halls, and it was home to craftsmen who had been taken from all the lands that the Mongols conquered. In the palace stood a silver tree that poured wine and other drinks from its branches, made by a French goldsmith named Guillaume Boucher, and the friar William of Rubruck described it in 1254. The Mongol court was a cosmopolitan place where a Frenchman could build a fountain for a khan.

European rulers, who were alarmed by the Mongol advance, sent friars to find out who these strangers were, and two of them, John of Plano Carpini in 1246 and William of Rubruck in 1253, wrote the first eyewitness accounts by Europeans. They described the felt tents, the strange food, the customs and the formidable discipline of the Mongols, and they brought back letters from the khans. Their books, written in plain and lively Latin, taught Europe how large the world really was.

Kublai Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, completed the conquest of China and in 1271 gave his dynasty the Chinese name Yuan, ruling from a new capital on the site of modern Beijing. His government used paper money backed by the state, and it astonished European visitors, who were used to carrying heavy bags of gold and silver. Marco Polo wrote with wonder that a sheet of paper could buy as much as a piece of gold.

In about 1271, a young man named Marco Polo left Venice with his father and uncle and travelled overland towards the court of the Mongol ruler Kublai Khan in China. Years later, his account of the journey became one of the most widely read books in Europe, filled with wonders that many readers refused to believe. Historians still argue about how much he saw with his own eyes and how much he heard from others.

After he returned to Italy, Marco Polo was captured in a naval war between Venice and Genoa and held in a Genoese prison, where he met a professional writer of romances named Rustichello. About 1298 Polo dictated his story to him, and the resulting book was copied by hand in many languages and was read across Europe for centuries. Even in his own day readers argued about it, and some wondered how many of its marvels were true.

While European friars were travelling east, a Christian monk named Rabban Sauma, who had been born near Beijing, travelled west. In 1287 and 1288 he journeyed to Europe on a diplomatic mission for the Mongol ruler of Persia, meeting the kings of France and England and the pope in Rome. He wrote a vivid account of the strange cities that he saw, for the road ran in both directions, and each traveller carried home a story about the unfamiliar world.

Roads carry misfortune as well as wealth, and the clearest proof came in the 1340s, when the plague known as the Black Death, which probably began in Central Asia, moved along trade routes towards the Black Sea. In 1347 merchant ships carried it to ports in Italy, and from there it spread across Europe, killing perhaps a third of the population, though estimates vary. Cities that lived by trade were often the first to suffer, for the same crossroads that brought them prosperity also brought the disease.

In 1377 the port of Ragusa, which is now called Dubrovnik, ordered that ships arriving from infected places must wait thirty days before anyone could land, and Venice later extended the wait to forty days. The Italian word for forty, quaranta, gave us our word quarantine, and the rule is one of the first public health measures that we know of. People did not yet understand how the disease spread, but they had noticed that it came by road and by ship.

After the plague had passed, there were far fewer workers than there had been before, and in many parts of Europe the survivors found that landowners and employers had to offer better pay. Trade, which had been interrupted, recovered over the following decades, and the towns slowly refilled. Historians still argue about the full effects of the disaster, but few doubt that it changed the way that people lived and worked.

Pepper came from southern India and cinnamon from Sri Lanka, but at that time cloves and nutmeg grew only on a handful of small islands in what is now Indonesia. They travelled thousands of kilometres by sea and land, through the hands of many sailors and merchants, before they reached a European kitchen. Their rarity and their long journey made them worth almost their weight in silver, and people found them irresistible for flavouring food, for preserving it and for perfume and medicine.

Venice grew rich by buying spices from the merchants of Egypt and Syria and selling them across Europe at a handsome profit, and its fleets of galleys carried them over the Mediterranean. The city's enormous shipyard, called the Arsenal, built vessels with such speed and organisation that it has often been compared with a factory. A trade that had begun in Indian forests ended in the palaces of Venice.

Portugal, a small country on the Atlantic coast, hoped to reach the spices by sea, and its captains sailed a little farther down the African coast with every voyage. In 1488 Bartolomeu Dias was blown around the southern tip of the continent by a storm and then turned back, because his crew refused to go on. The cape was later named the Cape of Good Hope, for it gave the Portuguese a good hope of reaching India.

European merchants wanted spices such as pepper, cinnamon and cloves without paying the many middlemen along the overland and Indian Ocean routes. In 1498 the Portuguese captain Vasco da Gama rounded the southern tip of Africa and reached Calicut on the coast of India, after a voyage of about ten months. Within a few years Portuguese ships were fighting for control of the main ports of the Indian Ocean.

A pilot from the East African coast, who knew the pattern of the monsoon, guided Gama's ships across the Indian Ocean to Calicut in 1498. The local ruler, who was used to merchants from Arabia and China, is said to have been unimpressed by the cheap gifts that the Portuguese had brought, and the Europeans were not made very welcome. Gama nevertheless returned home with a cargo of spices that was worth many times the cost of the voyage.

For centuries the Indian Ocean had been open to anyone who could sail it, but the Portuguese changed the rules by arriving with cannon on their ships. They seized the ports of Goa in 1510 and Malacca in 1511, built forts to guard them, and forced merchants of other nations to buy permits if they wished to trade. Violence had become a part of the business, and the era of armed trading companies had begun.

Lisbon soon became a great market for spices, and the Portuguese king, who liked to call himself the lord of the conquest and trade of India, grew very rich. Venice kept trading for many decades, however, and the old routes through Egypt did not disappear overnight, but the balance of European commerce was shifting from the Mediterranean towards the Atlantic. Historians now stress that the old and new roads existed side by side for a long time.

Christopher Columbus, a sailor from Genoa, believed that Asia lay only a short way to the west across the Atlantic, because he had badly underestimated the size of the Earth. For years he went from court to court asking for money, and he was refused several times before Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand of Spain agreed to pay for his ships. His calculations were wrong, but his determination was unshakeable, and it changed the history of the world.

Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain in 1492, believed that he could reach the riches of Asia by crossing the Atlantic Ocean to the west. He was wrong about the distance, and he arrived instead at islands in the Caribbean, in a part of the world that Europeans of the time did not know existed. His voyage began the permanent contact between the Americas and the rest of the world.

In October 1492 Columbus and his men waded ashore on a small island in the Bahamas, where they were met by the Taíno people, who had lived in the Caribbean for centuries. Columbus was convinced that he had reached the outer fringe of Asia, which Europeans called the Indies, so he called the islanders Indians, and the mistake has lasted ever since. For the people who lived there, the arrival of the ships was the start of a long disaster.

Ships also moved plants and animals across the oceans, and this great exchange transformed diets on every continent. Potatoes, maize, tomatoes, chilli peppers and cocoa went from the Americas to the rest of the world, while wheat, sugar cane, cattle and horses travelled the other way. Italian cooking without tomatoes and Indian cooking without chillies would both have been quite different.

The potato from the Andes proved to be a marvellous crop for Europe, because it grew well in cold, stony ground where wheat struggled and it produced more food from each hectare than grain did. Maize and sweet potatoes, meanwhile, became important in parts of Africa and China, and historians believe that these new foods helped populations to grow. The success of the potato had a dark side, as the Irish found when a disease destroyed the crop in the 1840s.

The ships carried a terrible cargo that nobody intended, for smallpox, measles and other diseases from the Old World spread among people who had never met them and had no immunity. Estimates vary widely, but historians agree that in many regions the majority of the population died within a century, and whole communities disappeared. It is the heaviest cost of the great exchange, and no list of its benefits should leave it out.

In 1519 five ships under the Portuguese captain Ferdinand Magellan left Spain, hoping to find a western way to the Spice Islands. They struggled for months through a strait at the tip of South America before entering a vast ocean that Magellan named the Pacific. Magellan was killed in the Philippines in 1521, but one ship, commanded by Juan Sebastián Elcano, continued westward and reached Spain in 1522 with eighteen men aboard, completing the first voyage around the world.

From 1565, Spanish galleons made regular voyages across the Pacific between Acapulco in Mexico and Manila in the Philippines, carrying silver from American mines to Asia. In return they brought back Chinese silk, porcelain and spices, which were then sent on across Mexico and the Atlantic to Spain. For the first time, a single trade linked Europe, Asia and the Americas in one great loop.

In the Andes, the mountain of Potosí, in what is now Bolivia, was found to be full of silver, and with the mines of Mexico it supplied most of the silver in the world. The metal was minted into coins that were used from Spain to China, where merchants and officials wanted silver for taxes and trade, and Chinese goods flowed out in exchange. Behind the wealth lay a harsh system of forced labour, in which a great many Indigenous workers lost their lives.

By about 1600 a web of sea routes connected every inhabited continent for the first time, and goods, plants, animals, diseases and ideas moved around it constantly. Wealthy families in Mexico City wore Chinese silk and ate from porcelain made in Chinese kilns, while Chinese merchants sold their wares for American silver. The world of the old overland road had grown into something much bigger, and the new roads were made of water.

In the mountains of southwest China, a network of steep paths known as the Tea Horse Road carried bricks of pressed tea to Tibet, where the drink had become a daily necessity. In return, Tibetan traders sent horses and mules, animals that China always needed for its armies. Porters carried enormous loads on their backs, climbing for weeks over passes thousands of metres high.

The porters of the Tea Horse Road carried towers of tea bricks wrapped in bamboo leaves, and some loads were said to weigh as much as the person who bore them. Each man carried a T-shaped stick, which he could wedge beneath his burden to rest without lowering it, since lifting it again on a steep path was the hardest part. Their work was so brutal that it wore out even the strongest of them.

In the cold, thin air of the Tibetan plateau, people drank tea mixed with butter and salt many times a day, for it warmed the body, supplied fat and eased the dryness of the climate. Since tea would not grow at such heights, every cup depended on caravans from the south, and the demand from the mountains was almost endless. Rarely has a drink been so closely tied to the shape of a road.

The Chinese government needed strong mountain horses for its armies and its postal service, and so it set up special offices where tea could be exchanged for them at fixed rates. The rates were often harsh, and in some periods a single good horse cost a very large amount of tea, which suggests how much the animals were wanted. The caravans of the Tea Horse Road were, in effect, an extension of imperial policy.

Mountain towns such as Lijiang, in Yunnan, prospered because the mule caravans of the Tea Horse Road had to stop there to rest, repair their harness and sell their goods. The old stone streets, worn smooth by centuries of hooves, are now walked by tourists, and the old courtyard inns still welcome travellers. A road may fade, but it often leaves its towns behind it like footprints.

In the Andes, the Inca built a network of roads of about thirty thousand kilometres, climbing mountains by stone steps and crossing gorges on bridges woven from grass. Since they had neither wheeled carts nor horses, the roads were made for walkers and llamas, and runners called chasquis passed messages from one relay post to the next. Without a conventional script, the empire held together largely because information could travel quickly by road.

The Inca called their empire Tawantinsuyu, which means the land of the four quarters, and its capital, Cusco, stood at the point where the four parts met. Four great roads led out from the central square towards the coast, the highlands, the forests and the distant south, so that every journey could be understood in terms of its relation to the capital. The Inca built their country as a wheel, with Cusco as its hub and the roads as its spokes.

Along the Inca roads, small huts stood every few kilometres, and in each of them young runners called chasquis waited ready to run. A messenger arriving in a hurry would blow a conch shell or shout the message, and the next man would take it and sprint to the following hut, so that news could travel enormous distances in a day. The system took advantage of the greatest asset the Inca possessed, which was an army of fit and willing people.

The Inca had no writing in the sense that we understand it, but they kept careful records on bundles of coloured cords tied with knots, called quipus, in which the colour, position and type of every knot carried meaning. Trained officials used them to count people, goods and taxes across the whole empire, and scholars still disagree about whether some of them may also have recorded stories. The knotted cord is a reminder that a road needs a record as well as a runner.

Where the road met a deep gorge, Inca engineers crossed it with a suspension bridge made of grass, twisting the straw into cables as thick as a man's body and weaving them into a swaying walkway. Because grass rots, the bridges had to be renewed every year, and at Q'eswachaka, in Peru, the nearby villages still gather each June to rebuild one in the traditional way. A road is kept alive by a community that takes care of it, and this is as true now as it was five hundred years ago.

The roads of history also carried cargoes that we should never forget, because for many centuries human beings were bought and sold along them. Enslaved people were marched across the Sahara, shipped across the Indian Ocean and forced across the Atlantic, and millions of lives were broken by trades that made other people rich. A fair history of roads must count this cost beside the silk, spices and ideas.

For many centuries, the caravans that carried salt, cloth and gold across the Sahara also carried captives, who had been taken in wars and raids in West and Central Africa. They were to be sold in the markets of the north, and the crossing was a harsh ordeal of heat, thirst and exhaustion that, historians believe, many did not survive. These caravans left few records of their own, so we know the story mostly from the accounts of those who profited.

On the East African coast, captives were loaded onto ships bound for Arabia, Persia and India, a trade that had existed for many centuries and grew rapidly in the nineteenth century, when the island of Zanzibar became its main market. Pressure from Britain and the work of campaigners finally led to the closing of the Zanzibar slave market in 1873, but illegal trading continued for some years afterwards. A cathedral now stands on the site where the market once was, and the old slave chambers can still be visited.

From the early sixteenth century, European merchants began shipping enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to work in the colonies of the Americas, and the trade continued, with growing cruelty, for about 350 years. Historians estimate that roughly twelve million people were forced aboard the ships, and most were taken from the coast of West and Central Africa, often after being captured inland and marched to the sea. It was the largest forced migration in history, and it was built on roads and sea lanes.

The voyage across the Atlantic was known as the Middle Passage, and it lasted from a few weeks to several months, during which the captives were packed tightly into the holds of ships with little air, food or water. Illness spread quickly in these crowded spaces, and historians believe that well over a million people died before the ships reached land. Survivors who were later able to write about it described the experience with great restraint, and their words still move us.

In the Americas, enslaved people were forced to plant, cut and process sugar, cotton, tobacco and coffee without pay or freedom, in conditions that often shortened their lives. The profits helped to make planters and merchants rich and to build whole port cities, such as Bristol, Liverpool and Nantes, which still contain fine buildings paid for in this way. The goods on a breakfast table in Europe, from sweet tea to cotton shirts, had often been produced by people who were not free.

Enslaved people never accepted their condition, and they resisted in every way they could, from working slowly and keeping their own songs and beliefs to open revolts and escapes to remote hills and forests, where they sometimes founded free communities. In Haiti, a great uprising which began in 1791 overthrew the French planters, ended slavery on the island and led, in 1804, to the creation of a free republic. It was the first nation in the world to be founded by formerly enslaved people, and it paid a heavy price for its freedom.

Campaigners in Britain and elsewhere, among them former slaves such as Olaudah Equiano who wrote powerful books about their lives, gathered petitions, spoke at meetings and organised boycotts of slave-grown sugar. Britain banned the slave trade in 1807 and slavery throughout its empire from 1833, the United States ended slavery in 1865 after a terrible civil war, and Brazil was the last country in the Americas to abolish it, in 1888. The struggle took generations, and the freedom that finally came was often incomplete and unequal for those who had waited so long.

In the United States, a secret network of safe houses, guides and helpers called the Underground Railroad helped thousands of enslaved people to escape from the South to the northern states and Canada. They travelled mostly at night and followed the stars, and a brave woman named Harriet Tubman, who had escaped herself, is believed to have returned to the South about thirteen times. She guided roughly seventy people to freedom, and these roads of hope were built entirely out of courage and trust.

Today memorials around the world remember the millions of people who were taken from Africa and those who died in bondage, and museums and schools tell the story in more detail than ever before. At Ouidah, in Benin, a monument called the Door of No Return stands near the sea where captives were once marched to the ships, and a United Nations project has encouraged research and remembrance since 1994. A fair account of the world's roads must include the painful ones, because we learn from them as well.

China's Grand Canal, begun in earlier centuries and joined into one great waterway in the early seventh century, linked the Yangtze river with the Yellow river and eventually ran for more than a thousand kilometres. Its main purpose was to carry grain from the rich rice country of the south to the capital and armies of the north. Parts of it are still used by barges today, more than a thousand years after the builders finished.

The Erie Canal, which opened in 1825, ran for more than five hundred kilometres across the state of New York and linked the Great Lakes with the Hudson river and the port of New York. Boats were pulled by mules walking along the towpath, and they moved goods at a fraction of the cost of a wagon, so farmers in the interior could sell their grain to the world. The canal helped to turn a small port into the greatest city of its country, and New York never looked back.

In 1825 the Stockton and Darlington Railway in the north of England opened as the first public line to use a steam locomotive, which pulled wagons of coal and carriages of passengers at the speed of a trotting horse. The Liverpool and Manchester Railway followed in 1830, and it was the first line to depend on steam power alone and to carry passengers on a regular timetable. Within twenty years, railway fever had swept across Europe and North America, and the whole pace of life had quickened.

Steamships freed sailors from their dependence on the wind, and in 1838 the Great Western crossed from Bristol to New York in about fifteen days, much faster than a typical sailing ship. Within a few decades steam had made schedules reliable, and passengers, letters and fresh news could cross the ocean on a regular timetable. A voyage that had been an adventure was becoming a routine, and the Atlantic was shrinking year by year.

Before the railways, each town kept its own local time, set by the position of the sun, so that clocks in Bristol and London differed by several minutes. Timetables could not work in such confusion, and so the British railways adopted a single standard time in the 1840s, while North American railways introduced time zones in 1883. The road was not only changing the map but also the way that people measured their days.

India's first passenger railway opened in 1853, running a short distance from Bombay to Thane, and within a few decades it had grown into one of the largest rail networks in the world. The lines were built under British rule, largely with British money and for British purposes, such as moving troops and carrying cotton and other raw materials to the ports, but they also carried millions of Indian passengers. A road can serve many purposes at once, and not all of them are the builder's.

On 10 May 1869, at a remote place called Promontory Summit in Utah, the Union Pacific line, which had been built westward from the Missouri river, met the Central Pacific line, which had been built eastward from California. A final spike of gold was hammered into the ground, a telegraph operator signalled the news across the country, and a journey from coast to coast that had taken months by wagon could now be made in about a week. The ceremony was celebrated with cannon and champagne, but the work had been done by thousands of labourers.

The Central Pacific line could not have been finished without many thousands of Chinese immigrants, who drilled and blasted tunnels through the granite of the Sierra Nevada. They worked through winters of terrible cold, and avalanches killed many of them, yet they were left out of the famous photograph of the golden spike ceremony. A road is only as good as the people who build it, and the story of these builders is now being told.

The Trans-Siberian Railway was built between 1891 and 1916 across the forests, rivers and frozen plains of Siberia, and it runs for more than nine thousand kilometres from Moscow to the Pacific port of Vladivostok. A passenger today needs about a week to cross a single country that spans eleven time zones, and the train passes Lake Baikal, the deepest lake on Earth. Its builders faced mud, ice, bridges over wide rivers and enormous distances, and they succeeded in joining two oceans.

Railway stations became the new crossroads of the modern world, and cities grew rapidly wherever several lines met, just as oasis towns had once grown wherever caravans stopped. Chicago, which had been a small settlement in the 1830s, became one of the largest cities in the United States, because dozens of railways brought grain, cattle and timber from the prairies and carried manufactured goods back. The patterns of the old roads were being repeated, this time with iron and steam, on a far larger scale.

The Suez Canal opened in 1869, after about ten years of digging led by the French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps, and it joined the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea across the narrow isthmus of Suez. Most of the labour was done by Egyptian workers, using simple tools and often under harsh conditions, and a great many of them died of accidents and disease. It was the project that Darius had hoped for more than two thousand years before.

The canal made the sea journey from London to India several thousand kilometres shorter, because ships no longer had to sail all the way around Africa, and steamers could use it much more easily than sailing ships. Trade between Europe and Asia grew rapidly, and the waterway quickly became one of the most important roads in the world. It has been a prize, a battlefield and a bottleneck ever since, and the world still holds its breath when ships are stuck there.

The French began a canal across Panama in the 1880s but gave up after fever, landslides and money problems had killed many thousands of workers, and the United States took over the project in 1904 and finished it in 1914. Tens of thousands of labourers, many of them from the Caribbean islands, dug through hills and jungle, and thousands more died from accidents and diseases such as yellow fever and malaria. Better knowledge of mosquitoes and the way that they carry disease made the final success possible.

The Panama Canal works like a staircase made of water, for huge locks lift each ship about twenty-six metres to an artificial lake in the middle of the isthmus and then lower it again on the other side. The shortcut saves more than ten thousand kilometres on a voyage from New York to San Francisco, which would otherwise have to pass around the stormy tip of South America. Water, not rock, was the great engineering problem, and the builders solved it with enormous steel gates that are still working today.

In the twentieth century the petrol engine put millions of people behind steering wheels, and engineers responded with smooth, surfaced highways that carried traffic at speeds no Roman could have imagined. Cities spread outward, suburbs appeared, and a worker could live thirty kilometres from the office. The road, once a slow track for feet and hooves, had become a machine of its own.

In 1908 the American manufacturer Henry Ford began to sell the Model T, a simple, strong and reasonably priced car. From 1913 his factory built it on a moving assembly line, in which each worker added a single part as the chassis passed by, and the price fell until millions of ordinary families could afford one. Cars had been a toy for the rich, and Ford made them a tool for everybody.

In 1956 the United States began to build its Interstate Highway System, which grew to more than seventy thousand kilometres of fast, wide roads with no crossroads and no traffic lights, and many other countries built motorways in the same decades. Lorries could now carry goods from one end of a continent to the other in a few days, and families could drive for a holiday that would once have taken a month. The Romans would have been astonished at the speed and also at the traffic jams.

On 17 December 1903, on a windy beach at Kitty Hawk in North Carolina, Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first successful flights in a powered, controlled aeroplane. The first flight lasted only twelve seconds and covered about thirty-seven metres, a distance shorter than the length of a modern jumbo jet, but the fourth flight of the day lasted nearly a minute. Within a lifetime, humanity had learned to travel on a road that no one had to build.

Aircraft added a third dimension to the story, for they needed no road at all, only an airport at each end. A journey from London to Delhi that once took many months by caravan and ship can now be made in less than a day, and in a normal year several billion passengers board flights. The sky is now crossed by invisible roads, planned as carefully as any Roman highway.

Airports have become the new crossroads, and a few giant hubs, such as those of London, Dubai and Singapore, connect most of the world's cities to one another. A traveller can now reach almost any city on Earth with one or two changes of plane, while freight aircraft carry fresh flowers, medicines and mobile phones overnight. Wherever a road network has a few places where everything meets, those places become rich, busy and crowded.

Until the 1950s, loading a ship was a slow business in which dock workers carried every barrel, sack and crate on board piece by piece, and a vessel might spend a week in port. A trucking owner from North Carolina named Malcolm McLean noticed how much time and money was wasted and began to think about a system in which the whole truck body could be lifted straight onto the ship. His idea sounds obvious now, but it overturned the working life of every port in the world.

In 1956 a converted tanker carried the first cargo of standard metal containers from New Jersey to Texas, and it began a quiet revolution. Because a box could be lifted by crane directly from ship to train to lorry without being opened, the cost of moving goods across oceans fell dramatically. Today a very large share of the things in our homes, from shoes to televisions, has crossed the sea inside such a box.

The key to the system was standardisation, for containers were built in a few agreed sizes, notably twenty and forty feet long, so that the same box fitted every ship, train, lorry and crane in the world. Cranes lifted a container in minutes, ships spent a day instead of a week in port, and shipping a television or a pair of shoes became so cheap that it hardly mattered where it was made. This is why the labels on our clothes now come from so many countries.

Today the largest container ships can carry more than twenty thousand boxes, and they measure almost four hundred metres from bow to stern, which is longer than most skyscrapers are tall. Together with a few thousand smaller vessels, they carry the great majority of the goods that cross the oceans, moving along sea lanes that are just as carefully chosen as any caravan track. Their crews are surprisingly small, and a whole ship can be steered by a few dozen people.

A single cotton shirt may be made from fibre grown in one country, spun into thread in a second, woven into cloth in a third, sewn in a fourth and shipped in a container to a shop in a fifth. At each step, goods move along a road, a railway or a sea lane that was planned by someone, and the final price of the garment hides the journey. Our world is so closely woven together that very few of us can name every country that has touched the clothes we wear.

In 1844, Samuel Morse sent a message from Washington to Baltimore along a telegraph wire, using a code of short and long signals, and the first words were What hath God wrought. Wires soon followed the railways across the United States and Europe, and for the first time news travelled faster than any horse, ship or train. For thousands of years a message could go no faster than the messenger, and now that rule was broken.

The first telegraph cable across the Atlantic was laid in 1858, and although it failed after a few weeks, a lasting one followed in 1866. Today, a web of cables no thicker than a garden hose lies on the sea floor, and almost all the data that passes between continents, from emails to video calls, flows through them. The newest roads of all are invisible, and most of us have never seen one.

Hundreds of undersea cables now cross the oceans, protected by a covering of steel and plastic where they come near the shore, but lying bare on the deep sea floor. Ship anchors and fishing gear sometimes break them, and special repair ships go out to lift the damaged cable on board, mend it and lower it again. Most of us never think about this quiet work, though we rely on it every time we send a message.

The roads carried language as surely as they carried cargo, and our everyday speech is full of passengers. The word sugar passed from Sanskrit through Persian and Arabic, algebra comes from the title of a ninth-century Arabic book, and coffee reached English by way of Turkish. Every time we use such words, we are walking, without noticing it, along an old trade route.

In many languages, from Russian and Persian to Turkish and Hindi, the drink is called chai, while in English, French and German it is some form of the word tea, and the difference is a map in miniature. The first form comes from the northern Chinese pronunciation, which travelled overland along the Silk Road, while the second comes from the pronunciation of the southern coast, which was carried by the ships of the sea trade. A single word, in other words, can still show which road a thing travelled, even after the road itself has gone.

A city at a crossroads can tax, supply and entertain everyone who passes through, and so places such as Venice, Samarkand, Istanbul and Singapore flourished where roads and sea lanes met. When the trade moved to another route, however, the fortunes of such cities could fall as quickly as they had risen. Geography offers the opportunity, but the choices of travellers and rulers decide who keeps it.

Singapore was founded as a British trading post in 1819, on a small island at the southern end of the Strait of Malacca, which is one of the narrowest and busiest sea lanes on Earth. A large share of the world's sea trade passes through the strait, and the city has grown into a great port, an airline hub and a financial centre by making itself useful to everyone who travels. Its history repeats the oldest lesson of the roads, which is that a place at a crossing can prosper by being open.

The fortunes of a road depend on those who protect it, and when empires weakened or quarrelled, caravans faced heavy taxes, bandits and closed borders. As ships grew larger and sea routes safer and cheaper, much of the long-distance trade shifted from camel to cargo ship, and many caravan towns slowly lost their importance. Historians disagree about exactly how quickly this happened and why, but the general direction of change is clear.

In the Taklamakan, towns such as Niya and Loulan were abandoned centuries ago, when rivers shifted away or the trade moved elsewhere, and the dry air and the drifting sand preserved their wooden houses, tools and written records almost intact. When archaeologists such as Aurel Stein began to dig in the early twentieth century, they found letters on wooden tablets, bundles of documents and even loaves of bread, as if the inhabitants had left only yesterday. The sand has been a better keeper of the past than many a museum.

In 2014, the cultural agency of the United Nations, UNESCO, recognised part of the old route as a World Heritage Site, naming a long corridor from the ancient Chinese capital to the mountains of Central Asia. The listing covers thirty-three places in China, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, including cities, temples, forts, tombs and caravan stations, and it is meant to protect them for future generations. A road that once carried goods now carries visitors who come to see where history happened.

Some old roads are alive again, because ordinary people have decided to walk them for pleasure, for reflection or for faith. The Camino de Santiago, a network of pilgrim paths leading to a cathedral in north-western Spain, has been used for about a thousand years and is now walked by hundreds of thousands of people every year. They sleep in the same villages as medieval pilgrims, and they discover, as those pilgrims did, that a long walk changes the traveller.

Every road in this story has carried both gifts and harms, for the same route that brought paper, numbers, medicines and food also brought plagues, armies and slave traders. A fair account does not simply admire the roads, nor does it simply condemn them, but notices who benefited, who paid and who was left out of the record. The roads themselves are neutral, and what they become depends on the choices of the travellers.

Look at the road outside your own door, for it is almost certainly connected to the stories in this book. It may follow a track that farmers, pilgrims or soldiers used a thousand years ago, and it joins, mile by mile, with highways that lead to every port and city on Earth. The whole world is stitched together by roads, rails, sea lanes, air routes and cables, and each began with someone who wanted to reach something far away.

New roads are being made in our own time, from more cables on the sea floor and a swarm of satellites overhead to fast trains that cross whole continents in a day. As the ice of the Arctic melts, ships may open new sea routes in the far north, though this brings its own risks for the climate and for the people who live there. Every generation imagines that the roads are finished, and every generation turns out to be wrong.

Every road in this book began with a person who wanted something that lay beyond the horizon: a tool, a spice, a cure, a faith or simply a view. The oldest footprints in Tanzania and the newest cable beneath the sea belong to one long story of curiosity and need. What the next roads will carry, and who will be allowed to travel them, is a question that is still waiting for its answer.
